Your organization uses Google Workspace, Google Cloud, and a third-party SIEM. You need to export events including user logins, successful logins, and failed logins to the SIEM. The logs must be ingested in real time or near real time. What should you do?

options.text: Poll Cloud Logging for authentication events using the gcloud logging read tool. Forward the events to the SIEM.
Configure Google Workspace to directly send logs to the API endpoint of the third-party SIEM.
Create a Cloud Storage bucket as a sink for all logs. Configure the SIEM to periodically scan the bucket for new log files.
Create a Cloud Logging sink to export relevant authentication logs to a Pub/Sub topic for SIEM subscription.

questions.explanation:
A filtered Cloud Logging sink can route the relevant authentication log entries to a Pub/Sub topic, which a SIEM can subscribe to. Cloud Logging publishes routed entries to Pub/Sub as it receives them; entries are generally available within seconds, making this the appropriate near-real-time third-party integration method.

**Learn more:** [View logs routed to Pub/Sub](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/pubsub?hl=en) · [Route log entries](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/routing/overview)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A customer has deployed an application on Compute Engine that leverages the elastic nature of cloud computing.  
  
How can you collaborate with Infrastructure Operations Engineers to best ensure that Windows Compute Engine VMs remain current with all the latest OS patches?

options.text: Build new base images when patches are available, and use a CI/CD pipeline to rebuild VMs, deploying incrementally.
Federate a Domain Controller into Compute Engine, and roll out weekly patches via Group Policy Object.
Use Deployment Manager to provision updated VMs into new serving Instance Groups (IGs).
Reboot all VMs during the weekly maintenance window and allow the StartUp Script to download the latest patches from the internet.

questions.explanation:
An immutable-infrastructure approach packages approved OS patches into a new base image and replaces instances through a CI/CD rollout. This makes every replacement VM reproducible and current, while incremental deployment limits service disruption. Compute Engine managed instance groups support rolling out a new instance template gradually and controlling disruption during the update.

**Learn more:** [Automatically apply VM configuration updates in a MIG](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instance-groups/rolling-out-updates-to-managed-instance-groups) · [Create custom Windows Server images](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/windows/creating-windows-os-image)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization uses Google Workspace as its primary identity provider for Google Cloud. Users in your organization originally created their own passwords. Following a recent security event, you need to strengthen password security. What should you do?

options.text: Conduct a security awareness training session, and set the password expiration settings to require more frequent updates.
Check the Enforce strong password box, and check Enforce password policy at the next sign-in.
Check the Enforce strong password box, and set the password expiration to occur more frequently.
Audit user activity for suspicious logins by using the audit and investigation tool.

questions.explanation:
Google Workspace can enforce strong passwords and require users to comply with the password policy at their next sign-in. This forces users whose existing passwords do not meet the strengthened policy to change them. Frequent password expiration is not the preferred security control; Google states that password expiration has shown little positive security impact.

**Learn more:** [Enforce and monitor password requirements for users](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/users/enforce-and-monitor-password-requirements-for-users?visit_id=639160308295936113-1406794192&hl=en&rd=1)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],While migrating your organization’s infrastructure to GCP, many users will need access to the GCP Console. The Identity Management team already has a well-established process for managing users and wants to continue using its existing Active Directory or LDAP server together with the existing SSO password.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Manually synchronize the data in Google domain with your existing Active Directory or LDAP server.
Use Google Cloud Directory Sync to synchronize the data in Google domain with your existing Active Directory or LDAP server.
Users sign in directly to the GCP Console using the credentials from your on-premises Kerberos compliant identity provider.
Users sign in using OpenID (OIDC) compatible IdP, receive an authentication token, then use that token to log in to the GCP Console.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Directory Sync synchronizes users and related directory data from an existing Active Directory or LDAP directory to the Google domain, allowing the existing directory to remain the authoritative user-management system. GCDS provisions identities rather than synchronizing passwords; an existing-password SSO experience is provided by configuring federation separately.

**Learn more:** [Active Directory user account provisioning](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/identity/federating-gcp-with-active-directory-synchronizing-user-accounts?hl=en) · [Active Directory single sign-on](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/identity/federating-gcp-with-active-directory-configuring-single-sign-on?hl=en)

questions.domain: Securing communications and establishing boundary protection
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization hosts a financial services application on Compute Engine instances for a third-party company. The third party's servers, which will consume the application, also run on Compute Engine in a separate Google Cloud organization. You must configure a secure network connection between the Compute Engine instances and meet these requirements:  
  
- The network connection must be encrypted.  
- Communication between servers must use private IP addresses.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Configure a Cloud VPN connection between your organization's VPC network and the third party's that is controlled by VPC firewall rules.
Configure a VPC peering connection between your organization's VPC network and the third party's that is controlled by VPC firewall rules.
Configure a VPC Service Controls perimeter around your Compute Engine instances, and provide access to the third party via an access level.
Configure an Apigee proxy that exposes your Compute Engine-hosted application as an API, and is encrypted with TLS which allows access only to the third party.

questions.explanation:
Cloud VPN establishes an IPsec VPN connection between the two VPC networks, encrypting traffic in transit while routing application traffic between the Compute Engine instances by using their private IP address ranges. VPC firewall rules can restrict the permitted traffic. [Cloud VPN overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/overview)

**Learn more:** [Cloud VPN overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization uses a microservices architecture built on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Recent security reviews recommend stronger controls over deployed container images to reduce potential vulnerabilities and preserve compliance. You need to implement an automated system using managed services so that only approved container images are deployed to the GKE clusters. What should you do?

options.text: Develop custom organization policies that restrict GKE cluster deployments to container images hosted within a specific Artifact Registry project where your approved images reside.

Enforce Binary Authorization in your GKE clusters. Integrate container image vulnerability scanning into the CI/CD pipeline and require vulnerability scan results to be used for Binary Authorization policy decisions.
Automatically deploy new container images upon successful CI/CD builds by using Cloud Build triggers. Set up firewall rules to limit and control access to instances to mitigate malware injection.

Build a system using third-party vulnerability databases and custom scripts to identify potential Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) in your container images. Prevent image deployment if the CVE impact score is beyond a specified threshold.

questions.explanation:
Binary Authorization enforces container-image deployment policy on GKE. It can require trusted attestations before an image is deployed; an attestation can certify that a required activity, including a vulnerability scan, was completed. Connecting vulnerability scanning to the CI/CD process and requiring its approved result through Binary Authorization policy decisions provides automated, deploy-time enforcement that only approved images reach GKE.

**Learn more:** [Binary Authorization overview](https://cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/overview) · [Attestations overview](https://cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/attestations)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are handling protected health information (PHI) for an electronic health record system. The privacy officer is concerned that sensitive data is retained in the analytics system. You must anonymize the sensitive data in a nonreversible way. In addition, the anonymized data must not retain the character set or length. Which Google Cloud solution should you use?

options.text: Cloud Data Loss Prevention with deterministic encryption using AES-SIV
Cloud Data Loss Prevention with format-preserving encryption
Cloud Data Loss Prevention with cryptographic hashing
Cloud Data Loss Prevention with Cloud Key Management Service wrapped cryptographic keys

questions.explanation:
Sensitive Data Protection cryptographic hashing is a one-way de-identification method that replaces the input with a cryptographic hash digest. Its encoded output does not preserve the original data’s character set or length, unlike format-preserving encryption; deterministic encryption and FPE can be re-identified with the original cryptographic key.

**Learn more:** [Pseudonymization | Sensitive Data Protection](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/pseudonymization) · [De-identifying sensitive data | Sensitive Data Protection](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/deidentify-sensitive-data)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are deploying regulated workloads in Google Cloud. The regulation includes requirements for data residency and data access. It also mandates that support be delivered from the same geographical location in which the data resides.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Enable Access Transparency Logging.
Deploy Assured Workloads.
Deploy resources only to regions permitted by data residency requirements.
Use Data Access logging and Access Transparency logging to confirm that no users are accessing data from another region.

questions.explanation:
Assured Workloads applies predefined control packages for regulated workloads, including regional data boundaries, controls over Google personnel access to customer data, and support-case assignment controls based on personnel attributes. Packages with support controls can route support cases to qualified personnel located within the applicable geography.

**Learn more:** [Overview of Assured Workloads](https://docs.cloud.google.com/assured-workloads/docs/overview) · [Personnel data access and support controls](https://docs.cloud.google.com/assured-workloads/docs/personnel-access-data-controls)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A batch job running on Compute Engine requires temporary write access to a Cloud Storage bucket. You want the batch job to use only the minimum permissions needed to complete its task. What should you do?

options.text: Create a service account with full Cloud Storage administrator permissions. Assign the service account to the Compute Engine instance.
Create a service account and embed a long-lived service account key file that has write permissions specified directly in the batch job script.
Create a service account with the storage.objectCreator role. Use service account impersonation in the batch job's code.
Grant the predefined storage.objectCreator role to the Compute Engine instance's default service account.

questions.explanation:
The `roles/storage.objectCreator` role provides permission to create objects while withholding permissions to view, delete, or overwrite them. A dedicated service account impersonated by the workload provides short-lived credentials, supporting temporary access without embedding a long-lived key or granting broad or persistent permissions to the default Compute Engine service account.

**Learn more:** [IAM roles for Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/iam-roles) · [Best practices for using service accounts securely](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/best-practices-service-accounts)

questions.domain: Securing communications and establishing boundary protection
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are on a security team that needs to ensure a Cloud Storage bucket in Project A is readable only from Project B. You also need to ensure that data in the Cloud Storage bucket cannot be accessed from, or copied to, Cloud Storage buckets outside the network, even when the user has the correct credentials.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Enable VPC Service Controls, create a perimeter with Project A and B, and include Cloud Storage service.
Enable Domain Restricted Sharing Organization Policy and Bucket Policy Only on the Cloud Storage bucket.
Enable Private Access in Project A and B networks with strict firewall rules to allow communication between the networks.
Enable VPC Peering between Project A and B networks with strict firewall rules to allow communication between the networks.

questions.explanation:
VPC Service Controls enforces a service perimeter that provides a defense layer independent of IAM, controlling Cloud Storage data movement across the perimeter. With Project A and Project B in the same perimeter and the Cloud Storage service protected, reads and bucket-to-bucket copies can occur inside the perimeter, while access and copies involving Cloud Storage resources outside the perimeter are denied even to principals with otherwise-valid credentials.

**Learn more:** [Overview of VPC Service Controls](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/overview) · [Supported products and limitations — Cloud Storage](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/supported-products?hl=en)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You run applications on Cloud Run and have already enabled Container Analysis for vulnerability scanning. However, you are concerned about having insufficient control over the applications that get deployed. You must ensure that only trusted container images are deployed on Cloud Run.  
  
What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Enable Binary Authorization on the existing Cloud Run service.
Set the organization policy constraint constraints/run.allowedBinaryAuthorizationPolicies to the list or allowed Binary Authorization policy names.
Enable Binary Authorization on the existing Kubernetes cluster.
Use Cloud Run breakglass to deploy an image that meets the Binary Authorization policy by default.
Set the organization policy constraint constraints/compute.trustedImageProjects to the list of projects that contain the trusted container images.

questions.explanation:
Binary Authorization is Cloud Run’s deploy-time control for allowing only container images that satisfy an authorization policy. Enabling it on the existing Cloud Run service enforces the policy for new revisions. Configuring the `run.allowedBinaryAuthorizationPolicies` organization-policy constraint to allow the required policy makes Binary Authorization mandatory, preventing Cloud Run developers from simply disabling the service-level enforcement.

**Learn more:** [Enable Binary Authorization for Cloud Run](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/run/enabling-binauthz-cloud-run) · [Require Binary Authorization for Cloud Run](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/run/requiring-binauthz-cloud-run?hl=en)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization stores record data in Cloud Storage. You must retain all record data for a minimum of seven years. This requirement must be permanent.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: 1. Identify buckets with record data.2. Apply a retention policy, and set it to retain for seven years.3. Monitor the bucket by using log-based alerts to ensure that no modifications to the retention policy occurs.

1. Identify buckets with record data.2. Apply a retention policy, and set it to retain for seven years.3. Remove any Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles that contain the storage buckets update permission.
1. Identify buckets with record data.2. Enable the bucket policy only to ensure that data is retained.3. Enable bucket lock.
1. Identify buckets with record data.2. Apply a retention policy and set it to retain for seven years.3. Enable bucket lock.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud Storage bucket retention policy enforces the seven-year retention period. Enabling Bucket Lock permanently prevents that retention policy from being removed or shortened, satisfying the permanent retention requirement.

**Learn more:** [Use and lock retention policies](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/using-bucket-lock?hl=en) · [Bucket Lock](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/bucket-lock)

options.text: Grant access to specific users to the VPC Service Controls to create a perimeter to access the Cloud Storage buckets. Configure Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) to authenticate users before they can access the data.
Configure IAM conditions based on IP address ranges. Require users to connect through a VPN. Implement endpoint verification software on user devices to check for basic compliance.

Create an access level in Access Context Manager that requires a device policy. Create a Context-Aware Access policy using this access level. Apply the policy to the VPC Service Controls perimeter that includes the Cloud Storage buckets.
Use Cloud Firewall rules to restrict access to the Cloud Storage buckets based on the source IP addresses. Require users to authenticate with a multi-factor authentication method.

questions.explanation:
Access Context Manager access levels can define contextual requirements based on device policy, including operating-system attributes, using device information from Chrome Enterprise Premium and Endpoint Verification. Applying the resulting access level to a VPC Service Controls perimeter that protects the Cloud Storage resources enables access only from requests that satisfy the trusted-device requirements, regardless of the user's network location.

**Learn more:** [Allow access to protected resources from outside a perimeter](https://cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/use-access-levels) · [Define access policies using access levels](https://cloud.google.com/access-context-manager/docs/define-access-policies)

An organization’s standard network and security review involves analyzing application transit routes, request handling, and firewall rules. It wants to let developer teams deploy new applications without the burden of this complete review.  
  
How should you advise the organization?

options.text: Use Forseti with Firewall filters to catch any unwanted configurations in production.
Mandate use of infrastructure as code and provide static analysis in the CI/CD pipelines to enforce policies.
Route all VPC traffic through customer-managed routers to detect malicious patterns in production.
All production applications will run on-premises. Allow developers free rein in GCP as their dev and QA platforms.

questions.explanation:
Infrastructure as code combined with static analysis and policy enforcement in CI/CD provides preventive security guardrails before deployment. It codifies approved network and firewall configurations, consistently checks proposed changes, and blocks deployments that violate policy, allowing teams to deploy independently without relying on a full manual review for each application.

**Learn more:** [Implement shift-left security](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/security/implement-shift-left-security) · [Preventative controls for acceptable resource configurations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/blueprints/security-foundations/preventative-controls)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company is deploying many containerized applications to GKE. Its current CI/CD pipeline uses Cloud Build to build container images, moves those images to Artifact Registry, and then deploys them to GKE. You must ensure that only images that have passed vulnerability scanning and satisfy specific corporate policies can be deployed. The process must be automated and integrated with the existing CI/CD pipeline. What should you do?

options.text: Configure a policy in Binary Authorization to use Artifact Analysis vulnerability scanning to only allow images that pass the scan to deploy to your GKE clusters.
Enable Artifact Analysis vulnerability scanning and regularly scan images in Artifact Registry. Remove any images that do not meet the vulnerability requirements before deployment.
Implement a custom script in the Cloud Build pipeline that uses a third-party vulnerability scanning tool. Fail the build if vulnerabilities are found.
Configure GKE to use only images from a specific, trusted Artifact Registry repository. Manually inspect all images before pushing them to this repository.

questions.explanation:
Binary Authorization enforces deployment policies for container images on GKE. Artifact Analysis supplies vulnerability information that Binary Authorization can use to control deployment, so policy-compliant, scanned images are allowed while images that fail the applicable requirements are blocked at admission time.

**Learn more:** [Binary Authorization overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/overview) · [Attestations overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/attestations)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization is preparing to build business services in Google Cloud for the first time. You need to determine where appropriate controls or policies should be applied. You must also identify which aspects of your cloud deployment Google manages. What should you do?

options.text: Model your deployment on the Google Enterprise foundations blueprint. Follow the blueprint exactly and rely on the blueprint to maintain the posture necessary for your business.
Use the Risk Manager tool in the Risk Protection Program to generate a report on your cloud security posture. Obtain cyber insurance coverage.
Subscribe to the Google Cloud release notes to keep up on product updates and when new services are available. Evaluate new services for appropriate use before enabling their API.

Study the shared responsibilities model. Depending on your business scenario, you might need to consider your responsibilities based on the location of your business offices, your customers, and your data.

questions.explanation:
The Google Cloud shared responsibility model defines the respective security responsibilities of Google and the customer. Customer responsibilities can also be affected by the locations of the organization, its customers, and its data, because regional laws and data-residency requirements can govern how data is processed and stored.

**Learn more:** [Shared responsibilities and shared fate on Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/security/shared-responsibility-shared-fate)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A customer’s company contains multiple business units. Each business unit functions independently and has its own engineering group. Your team needs visibility into every project created across the company and wants to organize their Google Cloud Platform (GCP) projects by the different business units. Each business unit also needs separate IAM permission sets.  
  
Which strategy should you use to satisfy these requirements?

options.text: Create an organization node, and assign folders for each business unit.
Establish standalone projects for each business unit, using gmail.com accounts.
Assign GCP resources in a project, with a label identifying which business unit owns the resource.
Assign GCP resources in a VPC for each business unit to separate network access.

questions.explanation:
An organization resource is the root of the Google Cloud resource hierarchy and provides centralized ownership and visibility of projects. Folders beneath the organization can represent individual business units, and IAM roles granted at a folder are inherited by the projects and resources within that folder, enabling distinct permission sets for each unit.

**Learn more:** [About resource hierarchy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/cloud-platform-resource-hierarchy) · [Access control for folders with IAM](https://cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/access-control-folders)

You need to audit network segmentation for your Google Cloud footprint. You currently run Production and Non-Production infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS) environments. All VM instances are deployed without service-account customization.  
  
After observing traffic in your custom network, you find that all instances can communicate freely " despite tag-based VPC firewall rules being in place to segment traffic properly " with a priority of 1000. What are the most likely reasons for this behavior?

options.text: All VM instances are missing the respective network tags.
All VM instances are residing in the same network subnet.
All VM instances are configured with the same network route.

A VPC firewall rule is allowing traffic between source/targets based on the same service account with priority 999. E . A VPC firewall rule is allowing traffic between source/targets based on the same service account with priority 1001.

questions.explanation:
Network-tag rules match only VM instances carrying the applicable network tags, so missing tags prevent the intended segmentation rules from applying. For VPC firewall rules, a lower priority number has higher precedence; thus, a service-account-based allow rule at priority 999 overrides a conflicting tag-based rule at priority 1000. A rule at priority 1001 has lower precedence.

**Learn more:** [VPC firewall rules](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewalls) · [Use VPC firewall rules](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/using-firewalls)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An employer needs to monitor how bonus compensation has changed over time to find employee outliers and address earning disparities. This work must be done without revealing any individual's sensitive compensation data, while still allowing the outlier to be identified reversibly.  
  
Which Cloud Data Loss Prevention API technique should be used to achieve this?

options.text: Generalization
Redaction
CryptoHashConfig
CryptoReplaceFfxFpeConfig

questions.explanation:
`CryptoReplaceFfxFpeConfig` uses format-preserving encryption to replace sensitive values with encrypted tokens. The tokens support analysis without exposing the original compensation values and can be re-identified using the appropriate cryptographic key, unlike cryptographic hashing, which is one-way.

**Learn more:** [Pseudonymization — Sensitive Data Protection](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/pseudonymization) · [De-identifying sensitive data — Sensitive Data Protection](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/deidentify-sensitive-data)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization uses a third-party identity provider (IdP) that requires only a username and password for authentication. You need to enforce 2-step verification (2SV) for the Super admins in Cloud Identity. What should you do?

options.text: Create an organizational unit (OU) for Super admins, and enable 2SV within Cloud Identity for the OU.
Collaborate with the third-party IdP to enable 2SV for Super admins while maintaining the current Cloud Identity configuration.
Implement monitoring tools to track the authentication methods used by Super admins in Cloud Identity. Alert on those not using 2SV.
Evaluate the 2SV options for Super admins offered by both the third-party IdP and Cloud Identity. Implement the solution that provides the strongest second factor.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An organization uses Google Cloud to process substantial volumes of location data for analysis and visualization. This location data could be sensitive. You must design a solution that securely stores and processes the location data, minimizes data-exposure risk, and complies with both regulatory guidelines and the organization's internal data-residency policies. What should you do?

options.text: Enable location restrictions on Compute Engine instances and virtual disk resources where the data is handled. Apply labels to tag geographic metadata for all stored data.

Use the Cloud Data Loss Prevention (Cloud DLP) API to scan for sensitive location data before any storage or processing. Create Cloud Storage buckets with global availability for optimal performance, relying on Cloud DLP results to filter and control data access.

Create regional Cloud Storage buckets with Object Lifecycle Management policies that limit data lifetime. Enable fine-grained access controls by using IAM conditions. Encrypt data with customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) generated within specific Cloud KMS key locations.

Store data within BigQuery in a specified region by using dataset location configuration. Use authorized views and row-level security to enforce geographic access restrictions. Encrypt data within BigQuery tables by using customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK).

questions.explanation:
Regional Cloud Storage buckets place object data in a specified geographic region, supporting data-residency requirements. Object Lifecycle Management can automatically delete data after its permitted retention period, reducing the duration of exposure. IAM Conditions enforce conditional, attribute-based access control, and Cloud Storage CMEK gives the organization control over encryption keys; the Cloud KMS key ring must be created in the same location as the bucket data it encrypts.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Storage bucket locations](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/bucket-locations) · [Cloud Storage customer-managed encryption keys](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/encryption/customer-managed-keys)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization uses a centralized identity provider to manage human and machine access. You want to use this existing identity-management system so on-premises applications can access Google Cloud without hard-coded credentials. What should you do?

options.text: Enable Secure Web Proxy. Create a proxy subnet for each region that Secure Web Proxy will be deployed. Deploy an SSL certificate to Certificate Manager. Create a Secure Web Proxy policy and rules that allow access to Google Cloud services.

Enable Workforce Identity Federation. Create a workforce identity pool and specify the on-premises identity provider as a workforce identity pool provider. Create an attribute mapping to map the on-premises identity provider token to a Google STS token. Create an IAM binding that binds the required role(s) to the external identity by specifying the project ID, workload identity pool, and attribute that should be matched.
Enable Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP). Configure IAP by specifying the groups and service accounts that should have access to the application. Grant these identities the IAP-secured web app user role.

Enable Workload Identity Federation. Create a workload identity pool and specify the on-premises identity provider as a workload identity pool provider. Create an attribute mapping to map the on-premises identity provider token to a Google STS token. Create a service account with the necessary permissions for the workload. Grant the external identity the Workload Identity user role on the service account.

questions.explanation:
Workload Identity Federation is designed for workloads running outside Google Cloud, including on-premises applications. It lets an external identity provider’s credentials be exchanged for short-lived Google Cloud credentials instead of using service account keys. A workload identity pool and provider establish trust with the external identity provider; attribute mappings identify the external workload; and granting `roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser` on a suitably authorized service account permits that workload to impersonate the service account.

**Learn more:** [Workload Identity Federation](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/workload-identity-federation) · [Service account impersonation](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/service-account-impersonation)

Your company stores sensitive data in Cloud Storage. You want an on-premises-generated key to be used in the encryption process.

Use the Cloud Key Management Service to manage a key encryption key (KEK).

questions.question: Within an IaaS shared security-responsibility model, for which two stack layers does the customer have shared responsibility? (Choose two.)

Network Security
Storage Encryption
Access Policies
Boot

questions.explanation:
IaaS providers secure the underlying hardware, but network security and storage encryption are shared concerns: the provider supplies and secures the infrastructure and controls, while the customer configures network protections and encryption settings, including data and key-management choices. Access policies are configured by the customer.\

options.text: Set up Cloud Directory Sync to sync groups, and set IAM permissions on the groups.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to centralize logs for your team’s production projects and want the team to search and analyze them with Logs Explorer. What should you do?

options.text: Enable Cloud Monitoring workspace, and add the production projects to be monitored.
Use Logs Explorer at the organization level and filter for production project logs.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization aims to be a market leader in software innovation. You have provisioned a large number of Google Cloud environments so developers can test integration of Gemini in Vertex AI with their existing applications or build new projects. Your organization has 200 developers and a five-person security team. You need to prevent and detect appropriate security policies across the Google Cloud environments. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Apply organization policy constraints. Detect and monitor drifts by using Security Health Analytics.
Publish internal policies and clear guidelines to securely develop applications.
Use Cloud Logging to create log filters to detect misconfigurations. Trigger Cloud Run functions to remediate misconfigurations.
Apply a predefined AI-recommended security posture template for Gemini in Vertex AI in Security Command Center Enterprise or Premium tiers.
Implement the least privileged access Identity and Access Management roles to prevent misconfigurations.

questions.explanation:
Organization Policy constraints enforce preventative guardrails across Google Cloud resources, while Security Health Analytics supplies detective controls for security configuration issues. Security Command Center Premium or Enterprise includes the predefined Secure AI recommendations, essentials posture for Gemini and Vertex AI workloads; it combines organization policies with Security Health Analytics detectors and supports monitoring for posture drift at scale.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A security audit identified several inconsistencies in your project's Identity and Access Management (IAM) configuration. Some service accounts hold excessively permissive roles, and several external collaborators have more access than needed. You need detailed visibility into IAM policy changes, user activity, service account behavior, and access to sensitive projects. What should you do?

options.text: Configure Google Cloud Functions to be triggered by changes to IAM policies. Analyze changes by using the policy simulator, send alerts upon risky modifications, and store event details.
Enable the metrics explorer in Cloud Monitoring to follow the service account authentication events and build alerts linked on it.
Use Cloud Audit Logs. Create log export sinks to send these logs to a security information and event management (SIEM) solution for correlation with other event sources.
Deploy the OS Config Management agent to your VMs. Use OS Config Management to create patch management jobs and monitor system modifications.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Audit Logs records administrative and access activities across Google Cloud resources. Admin Activity logs include IAM permission changes, and Data Access logs can provide resource-access visibility when enabled. IAM audit logging includes service account events, while Cloud Logging sinks can route the audit logs to a SIEM for correlation with other security data sources.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Audit Logs overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/audit) · [Identity and Access Management audit logging](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/audit-logging)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization runs applications across multiple clouds. The applications need access to a Google Cloud resource running in your project. You must use short-lived access credentials to preserve security across the clouds. What should you do?

options.text: Create a managed workload identity. Bind an attested identity to the Compute Engine workload.
Create a service account key. Download the key to each application that requires access to the Google Cloud resource.
Create a workload identity pool with a workload identity provider for each external cloud. Set up a service account and add an IAM binding for impersonation.
Create a VPC firewall rule for ingress traffic with an allowlist of the IP ranges of the external cloud applications.

questions.explanation:
Workload Identity Federation lets external workloads exchange their cloud-native identities for short-lived Google Cloud credentials without using service account keys. Configure a workload identity pool and a provider for each external cloud, then grant the federated principals permission to impersonate a service account that has the required access to the Google Cloud resource.

**Learn more:** [Workload Identity Federation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/workload-identity-federation) · [Configure Workload Identity Federation with AWS or Azure VMs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/workload-identity-federation-with-other-clouds)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for a large organization that recently deployed a 100GB Cloud Interconnect connection between Google Cloud and your on-premises edge router. During routine connectivity checks, you observe that the connection is operational, but an error indicates that MACsec is operationally down. You need to resolve this error. What should you do?

options.text: Ensure that the Cloud Interconnect connection supports MACsec.
Ensure that the on-premises router is not down.
Ensure that the active pre-shared key created for MACsec is not expired on both the on-premises and Google edge routers.
Ensure that the active pre-shared key matches on both the on-premises and Google edge routers.

questions.explanation:
An operationally down MACsec session can result when the active MACsec keys on the on-premises router and Google’s edge routers do not match. The active CAK and CKN values must match on both sides. MACsec pre-shared keys have infinite validity, so key expiration is not the relevant condition.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshoot MACsec | Cloud Interconnect](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/how-to/macsec/troubleshoot-macsec) · [Enable MACsec | Cloud Interconnect](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/how-to/macsec/enable-macsec)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your security team uses encryption keys to maintain the confidentiality of user data. You want to define a process that reduces the effects of a potentially compromised symmetric encryption key in Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS).  
  
Which actions should your team take before an incident happens? (Choose two.)

options.text: Disable and revoke access to compromised keys.
Enable automatic key version rotation on a regular schedule.
Manually rotate key versions on an ad hoc schedule.
Limit the number of messages encrypted with each key version.
Disable the Cloud KMS API.

questions.explanation:
For symmetric encryption, automatically rotating key versions on a regular schedule is a recommended security practice that reduces the potential consequences of key compromise. Restricting the number of messages encrypted by a given key version also limits cryptanalytic exposure and the impact if that version is compromised.

**Learn more:** [Cloud KMS key rotation](https://cloud.google.com/kms/docs/key-rotation) · [Cloud KMS CMEK best practices](https://cloud.google.com/kms/docs/cmek-best-practices)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization is introducing a new continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD) process to deploy infrastructure and applications in Google Cloud. Many teams will use their own instances of the CI/CD workflow. It will run on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). The CI/CD pipelines must securely access Google Cloud APIs.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: 1. Create two service accounts, one for the infrastructure and one for the application deployment.2. Use workload identities to let the pods run the two pipelines and authenticate with the service accounts.3. Run the infrastructure and application pipelines in separate namespaces.

1. Create a dedicated service account for the CI/CD pipelines.2. Run the deployment pipelines in a dedicated nodes pool in the GKE cluster.3. Use the service account that you created as identity for the nodes in the pool to authenticate to the Google Cloud APIs.

1. Create individual service accounts for each deployment pipeline.2. Add an identifier for the pipeline in the service account naming convention.3. Ensure each pipeline runs on dedicated pods.4. Use workload identity to map a deployment pipeline pod with a service account.

1. Create service accounts for each deployment pipeline.2. Generate private keys for the service accounts.3. Securely store the private keys as Kubernetes secrets accessible only by the pods that run the specific deploy pipeline.

questions.explanation:
Workload Identity Federation for GKE is the recommended method for GKE workloads to authenticate to Google Cloud APIs. It supports distinct, fine-grained identities and permissions for individual workloads without service-account key files. Giving every deployment pipeline its own service account and mapping that pipeline’s pod identity enforces least privilege and isolates one team’s pipeline permissions from another’s. Using node identities would share credentials among workloads on a node, and storing private service-account keys in Kubernetes Secrets introduces avoidable key-management risk.

**Learn more:** [About Workload Identity Federation for GKE](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/workload-identity) · [Best practices for using Workload Identity Federation](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/best-practices-for-using-workload-identity-federation)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A customer has an on-premises Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) with a certificate authority (CA). You must issue certificates for numerous HTTP load-balancer frontends. The on-premises PKI should have minimal impact because it involves many manual processes, and the solution must scale.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use Certificate Manager to issue Google managed public certificates and configure it at HTTP the load balancers in your infrastructure as code (IaC).
Use a subordinate CA in the Google Certificate Authority Service from the on-premises PKI system to issue certificates for the load balancers.
Use Certificate Manager to import certificates issued from on-premises PKI and for the frontends. Leverage the gcloud tool for importing.

Use the web applications with PKCS12 certificates issued from subordinate CA based on OpenSSL on-premises. Use the gcloud tool for importing. Use the External TCP/UDP Network load balancer instead of an external HTTP Load Balancer.

questions.explanation:

options.text: Create a policy that requires employees to not leave their sessions open for long durations.

Generalization

questions.explanation:
Format-preserving encryption de-identifies a value by replacing it with an encrypted token that preserves its format and supports referential integrity. It can be re-identified with the original cryptographic key, allowing protected compensation data to be analyzed over time and an outlier to be identified when authorized. Cryptographic hashing is not reversible.

**Learn more:** [Transformation reference — Sensitive Data Protection](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/transformations-reference) · [Pseudonymization — Sensitive Data Protection](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/pseudonymization)

questions.domain: Securing communications and establishing boundary protection
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing a secure network architecture. You must completely isolate the development and production environments and prevent all network traffic between them. The network team requires only one central entry point from the on-premises environment into the cloud network. What should you do?

options.text: Create one Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network per environment. Add the on-premises entry point to the production VPC. Peer the VPCs with each other and create firewall rules to prevent traffic.
Create one shared Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network and use it as the entry point to the cloud network. Create separate subnets per environment. Create firewall rules to prevent traffic.
Create one Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network per environment. Create a VPC Service Controls perimeter per environment and add one environment VPC to each.
Create one Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network per environment. Create one additional VPC for the entry point to the cloud network. Peer the entry point VPC with the environment VPCs.

questions.explanation:
Use a separate VPC for each environment and a third VPC as the central on-premises entry point. Peer that entry VPC independently with each environment VPC. Google Cloud VPC Network Peering is non-transitive, so development and production do not gain a network path to one another through the entry-point VPC, while each can use the single centralized on-premises connection.

**Learn more:** [VPC Network Peering](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/vpc-peering)

questions.domain: Securing communications and establishing boundary protection
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are implementing communication restrictions for particular services in your Google Cloud organization. Your data analytics team operates in a dedicated folder. You must ensure that access to BigQuery is controlled for that folder and its projects. The data analytics team must be able to manage the restrictions only at the folder level. What should you do?

options.text: Create an organization-level access policy with a service perimeter to restrict BigQuery access. Assign the data analytics team the Access Context Manager Editor role on the access policy to allow the team to configure the access policy.

Create a scoped policy on the folder with a service perimeter to restrict BigQuery access. Assign the data analytics team the Access Context Manager Editor role on the scoped policy to allow the team to configure the scoped policy.

Define a hierarchical firewall policy on the folder to deny BigQuery access. Assign the data analytics team the Compute Organization Firewall Policy Admin role to allow the team to configure rules for the firewall policy.

Enforce the Restrict Resource Service Usage organization policy constraint on the folder to restrict BigQuery access. Assign the data analytics team the Organization Policy Administrator role to allow the team to manage exclusions within the folder.

questions.explanation:
A folder-scoped access policy with a VPC Service Controls service perimeter can protect BigQuery resources in projects under that folder. IAM can be delegated directly on the scoped policy, allowing the team to configure that policy's service perimeters while preventing it from administering the organization-level Access Context Manager policy.

**Learn more:** [Scoped policies | Access Context Manager](https://docs.cloud.google.com/access-context-manager/docs/scoped-policies) · [Create a scoped access policy | VPC Service Controls](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/manage-policies)

questions.question:
A DevOps team plans to create a new container that will run on Google Kubernetes Engine. Because the application will be internet-facing, they want to reduce the container's attack surface.  
  
What should they do?

options.text: Use Cloud Build to build the container images.
Build small containers using small base images.
Delete non-used versions from Container Registry.
Use a Continuous Delivery tool to deploy the application.

questions.explanation:
Small containers based on minimal images include only the application and necessary runtime dependencies, removing unnecessary packages and tools that could introduce vulnerabilities. This directly reduces the container attack surface.\
\
**Learn more:** [General development tips — Google Cloud documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/enterprise/knative-serving/docs/tips/general)

questions.question:
A DevOps team plans to create a new container that will run on Google Kubernetes Engine. Because the application will be internet-facing, they want to reduce the container's attack surface.  
  
What should they do?

options.text: Use date shifting with the context set to the unique ID of the test subject.
Extract the date using TimePartConfig from each date field and append a random month and year.
Use bucketing to shift values to a predetermined date based on the initial value.
Use the FFX mode of format preserving encryption (FPE) and maintain data consistency.

questions.explanation:
Date shifting randomly offsets dates while preserving the sequence and duration of a period. Setting the context to each test subject's unique ID makes the same shift apply to that subject's start and end dates, retaining the medication interval while concealing the original dates.

**Learn more:** [Date shifting | Sensitive Data Protection | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/concepts-date-shifting) · [Transformation reference | Sensitive Data Protection | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/transformations-reference)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization needs to publish yearly reports of website-usage analytics. You must ensure that no personally identifiable information (PII) is published by using the Cloud Data Loss Prevention (Cloud DLP) API. Data integrity must be retained. What should you do?

options.text: Detect all PII in storage by using the Cloud DLP API. Create a cloud function to delete the PII.
Discover and quarantine your PII data in your storage by using the Cloud DLP API.
Discover and transform PII data in your reports by using the Cloud DLP API.
Encrypt the PII from the report by using the Cloud DLP API.

questions.explanation:
Cloud DLP can discover PII and de-identify it through transformations before the reports are published. Appropriate transformations can remove or replace identifying values while maintaining the data’s analytical utility and, with cryptographic transformations, referential integrity.

**Learn more:** [De-identifying sensitive data](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/deidentify-sensitive-data) · [Pseudonymization](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/pseudonymization)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An administrative application runs on a virtual machine (VM) in a managed group on port 5601 within a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) instance that currently has no internet access. You need to expose the web interface on port 5601 to users and enforce authentication and authorization using Google credentials.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Configure the bastion host with OS Login enabled and allow connection to port 5601 at VPC firewall. Log in to the bastion host from the Google Cloud console by using SSH-in-browser and then to the web application.
Modify the VPC routing with the default route point to the default internet gateway. Modify the VPC Firewall rule to allow access from the internet 0.0.0.0/0 to port 5601 on the application instance.

Configure Secure Shell Access (SSH) bastion host in a public network, and allow only the bastion host to connect to the application on port 5601. Use a bastion host as a jump host to connect to the application.

Configure an HTTP Load Balancing instance that points to the managed group with Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) protection with Google credentials. Modify the VPC firewall to allow access from IAP network range.

questions.explanation:
Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) on an HTTP(S) load balancer authenticates users with Google credentials and authorizes access through IAM. An external Application Load Balancer can use a managed instance group as its backend, while VPC firewall rules restrict backend access to the required Google load-balancing and IAP infrastructure ranges rather than permitting direct public access.

**Learn more:** [Set up an external Application Load Balancer with IAP](https://cloud.google.com/iap/docs/load-balancer-howto) · [Identity-Aware Proxy overview](https://cloud.google.com/iap/docs/concepts-overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to ensure that data in your organization's Cloud Storage buckets cannot be publicly accessible from the internet. You want to enforce this for all Cloud Storage buckets. What should you do?

options.text: Remove Owner roles from end users, and configure Cloud Data Loss Prevention.
Remove Owner roles from end users, and enforce domain restricted sharing in an organization policy.
Configure uniform bucket-level access, and enforce domain restricted sharing in an organization policy.
Remove *.setIamPolicy permissions from all roles, and enforce domain restricted sharing in an organization policy.

questions.explanation:
Uniform bucket-level access disables Cloud Storage bucket and object ACLs, so access is governed only by IAM. Domain-restricted sharing limits which principals can be added to IAM allow policies, preventing public principals such as `allUsers` and `allAuthenticatedUsers` from receiving access. This combination closes both ACL-based and IAM-based public-access paths.

**Learn more:** [Uniform bucket-level access](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/uniform-bucket-level-access) · [Restrict identities with domain-restricted sharing](https://docs.cloud.google.com/organization-policy/restrict-domains)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your multinational organization is rapidly expanding in Google Cloud. New teams and projects are being added often. You are concerned about inconsistent application of security policies and permission sprawl throughout the organization. You must enforce consistent standards while preserving the autonomy of regional teams. You need to design a strategy that effectively manages IAM and organization policies at scale, ensuring security and administrative efficiency. What should you do?

options.text: Create detailed organization-wide policies for common scenarios. Instruct teams to apply the policies carefully at the project and resource level as needed.
Delegate the creation of organization policies to regional teams. Centrally review these policies for compliance before deployment.
Define a small set of essential organization policies. Supplement these policies with a library of optional policy templates for teams to leverage as needed.
Use a hierarchical structure of folders. Implement template-based organization policies that cascade down, allowing limited customization by regional teams.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud folders provide policy inheritance points and administrative boundaries. IAM roles and Organization Policies applied at an organization or folder level are inherited by descendant resources, which centralizes essential guardrails and reduces repeated per-project permissions. Folder-level delegation and controlled policy overrides allow regional teams to operate independently within centrally defined limits.

**Learn more:** [About resource hierarchy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/cloud-platform-resource-hierarchy) · [Organization Policy overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/organization-policy/overview)

questions.domain: Securing communications and establishing boundary protection
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization is rolling out a new web application on Compute Engine and requires strong perimeter security. You must safeguard the application against common web attacks, including SQL injection and cross-site scripting (XSS), while also controlling network traffic according to source IP address and user identity. What should you do?

options.text: Implement Cloud Load Balancing and Cloud DNS. Set up Cloud CDN to cache content and mitigate some DDoS attacks. Configure Cloud Armor to provide layer 7 protection.

Deploy Cloud Armor with its default WAF rules enabled. Configure network firewall rules on the Compute Engine instances to control all traffic based on source IP addresses. Use Cloud IAM to manage which users have roles granting access to the web application.

Use Google Cloud Armor with pre-configured WAF rules to filter malicious traffic. Implement VPC Service Controls to create a secure perimeter around the application's resources. Manage users with Cloud IAM.
Deploy Cloud Armor, and configure Cloud Firewall rules to control traffic based on source IP addresses. Integrate with Identity-Aware Proxy to control access based on user identity.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Armor provides layer-7 web application firewall protection, including rules for SQL injection and cross-site scripting. Cloud Firewall rules can restrict network traffic using source IP address criteria. Identity-Aware Proxy authenticates users and enforces authorization for protected Compute Engine web applications, providing identity-based application access.

**Learn more:** [Google Cloud Armor preconfigured WAF rules overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/waf-rules?hl=en) · [Identity-Aware Proxy overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iap/docs/concepts-overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You want to authenticate with the `gcloud` command-line tool by using a third-party single sign-on (SSO) SAML identity provider. Which options are required to make sure authentication is supported by the third-party identity provider (IdP)? (Choose two.)

options.text: SSO SAML as a third-party IdP
Identity Platform
OpenID Connect
Identity-Aware Proxy
Cloud Identity

questions.explanation:
Cloud Identity supports SAML 2.0 single sign-on with Google as the SAML service provider and an external organization IdP as the SAML identity provider. Therefore, the configuration requires a third-party SAML SSO IdP and Cloud Identity. OpenID Connect, Identity Platform, and Identity-Aware Proxy are not required for this SAML-based `gcloud` sign-in configuration.

**Learn more:** [Single sign-on | Cloud Architecture Center](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/identity/single-sign-on) · [Cloud Identity editions](https://cloud.google.com/identity/docs/editions)

You intend to deploy cloud infrastructure through a CI/CD cluster hosted on Compute Engine. You want to reduce the risk that a third party steals its credentials. What should you do?

options.text: Create a dedicated Cloud Identity user account for the cluster. Use a strong self-hosted vault solution to store the user's temporary credentials.
Create a dedicated Cloud Identity user account for the cluster. Enable the constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountCreation organization policy at the project level.
Create a custom service account for the cluster. Enable the constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation organization policy at the project level
Create a custom service account for the cluster. Enable the constraints/iam.allowServiceAccountCredentialLifetimeExtension organization policy at the project level.

questions.explanation:
A Compute Engine workload should authenticate using a dedicated user-managed service account attached to the instances, so it can obtain credentials without embedding user credentials or secret keys in code or configuration. Enforcing `constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation` prevents creation of external service-account keys, which are a credential-leakage risk.

**Learn more:** [Service accounts | Compute Engine](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/access/service-accounts) · [Organization policy constraints](https://cloud.google.com/organization-policy/reference/org-policy-constraints)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team has configured a Shared VPC network with project `co-vpc-prod` as the host project. The team configured the firewall rules, subnets, and VPN gateway in the host project. They must allow Engineering Group A to attach a Compute Engine instance to only the `10.1.1.0/24` subnet.  
  
What should the team grant Engineering Group A to meet this requirement?

options.text: Compute Network User Role at the host project level.
Compute Network User Role at the subnet level.
Compute Shared VPC Admin Role at the host project level.
Compute Shared VPC Admin Role at the service project level.

questions.explanation:
The Compute Network User role (`roles/compute.networkUser`) can be granted directly on a Shared VPC subnet, allowing a principal to create resources that use only that subnet. A host-project-level grant would allow use of all present and future subnets in the host project, so subnet-level IAM provides the required least-privilege access.

**Learn more:** [Provision Shared VPC](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/provisioning-shared-vpc)
