questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to connect your organization's on-premises network to an existing Google Cloud environment that contains one Shared VPC with two subnets named Production and Non-Production. You must:  
  
- Use a private transport link.  
- Configure access to Google Cloud APIs through private API endpoints from on-premises environments.  
- Ensure that Google Cloud APIs are consumed only through VPC Service Controls.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: 1. Set up a Cloud VPN link between the on-premises environment and Google Cloud. 2. Configure private access using the restricted.googleapis.com domains in on-premises DNS configurations.
1. Set up a Partner Interconnect link between the on-premises environment and Google Cloud. 2. Configure private access using the private.googleapis.com domains in on-premises DNS configurations.
1. Set up a Direct Peering link between the on-premises environment and Google Cloud. 2. Configure private access for both VPC subnets.

1. Set up a Dedicated Interconnect link between the on-premises environment and Google Cloud. 2. Configure private access using the restricted.googleapis.com domains in on-premises DNS configurations.

questions.explanation:
Dedicated Interconnect provides dedicated private connectivity from an on-premises network to a Google Cloud VPC. For Private Google Access from on-premises hosts when API consumption must be limited to services supported by VPC Service Controls, requests must be routed through the VPC and resolved to the restricted VIP using `restricted.googleapis.com`. This endpoint denies access to Google APIs and services that are not supported by VPC Service Controls; `private.googleapis.com` does not provide that restriction.

**Learn more:** [Private Google Access with VPC Service Controls](https://cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/private-connectivity) · [Configure Private Google Access for on-premises hosts](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/configure-private-google-access-hybrid)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization handles sensitive health information and needs to ensure that data is encrypted while it is in use by virtual machines (VMs). You must create a policy enforced throughout the entire organization.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Implement an organization policy that ensures that all VM resources created across your organization use customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) protection.
Implement an organization policy that ensures all VM resources created across your organization are Confidential VM instances.
Implement an organization policy that ensures that all VM resources created across your organization use Cloud External Key Manager (EKM) protection.
No action is necessary because Google encrypts data while it is in use by default.

questions.explanation:
Confidential VM encrypts sensitive code and data in memory while it is being processed, providing encryption in use. An organization policy can require all VM instances created across the organization to use Confidential VM. CMEK and Cloud EKM address encryption-key control for data at rest, rather than memory encryption during processing.

**Learn more:** [About Confidential VM](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/about-confidential-vm) · [Enforce Confidential VM use](https://cloud.google.com/confidential-computing/confidential-vm/docs/enforce-confidential-vm-use)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company is building a new application for your organization. The application includes two Cloud Run services: service A and service B. Service A delivers a web-based user frontend. Service B delivers backend services called by service A. You must configure Identity and Access Management for the application. The solution must follow the principle of least privilege. What should you do?

options.text: Create two separate service accounts. Grant one service account the permissions to execute service A, and grant the other service account the permissions to execute service B. Require authentication for service B. Permit only the service account for service A to call the backend.

Create three separate service accounts. Grant one service account the permissions to execute service A. Grant the second service account the permissions to run service Grant the third service account the permissions to communicate between both services A and Require authentication for service Call the backend by authenticating with a service account key for the third service account.
Create a new service account with the permissions to run service A and service B. Require authentication for service B. Permit only the new service account to call the backend.
Use the Compute Engine default service account to run service A and service B. Require authentication for service B. Permit only the default service account to call the backend.

questions.explanation:
A separate runtime service account for each Cloud Run service isolates their identities and permissions. Service B should require authentication, with only Service A’s service account granted the Cloud Run Invoker role on Service B; this permits the required frontend-to-backend call without granting broader access or sharing credentials.

**Learn more:** [Authenticating service-to-service | Cloud Run](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/authenticating/service-to-service) · [Introduction to service identity | Cloud Run](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/securing/service-identity)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization operates in a highly regulated environment and has a stringent set of compliance requirements to protect customer data. You must encrypt data while it is in use to meet regulations. What should you do?

options.text: Enable the use of customer-supplied encryption keys (CSEK) keys in the Google Compute Engine VMs to give your organization maximum control over their VM disk encryption.
Establish a trusted execution environment with a Confidential VM.
Use a Shielded VM to ensure a secure boot with integrity monitoring for the application environment.
Use customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) and Cloud KSM to enable your organization to control their keys for data encryption in Cloud SQL.

questions.explanation:
Confidential VMs use hardware-based memory encryption and provide a trusted execution environment (TEE), protecting sensitive code and data while they are being processed. This supplies encryption in use, unlike customer-managed or customer-supplied keys, which govern encryption at rest, and Shielded VMs, which protect boot integrity.

**Learn more:** [About Confidential VM](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/about-confidential-vm) · [Confidential Computing overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/confidential-computing/docs/confidential-computing-overview)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization runs Virtual Machines (VMs) with only private IP addresses in the Virtual Private Cloud (VPC), with internet access provided through Cloud NAT. Every day, you must patch all VMs with critical OS updates and provide summary reports.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Validate that the egress firewall rules allow any outgoing traffic. Log in to each VM and execute OS specific update commands. Configure the Cloud Scheduler job to update with critical patches daily for daily updates.
Copy the latest patches to the Cloud Storage bucket. Log in to each VM, download the patches from the bucket, and install them.

Assign public IPs to VMs. Validate that the egress firewall rules allow any outgoing traffic. Log in to each VM, and configure a daily cron job to enable for OS updates at night during low activity periods.
Ensure that VM Manager is installed and running on the VMs. In the OS patch management service, configure the patch jobs to update with critical patches dally.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud VM Manager Patch uses the OS Config agent to automate OS patch deployments across VM fleets, supports recurring schedules and critical patch classifications, and provides patch-compliance and patch-job reporting. Private-only VMs can retrieve updates through Cloud NAT, so public IP addresses and manual per-VM updates are unnecessary.

**Learn more:** [About Patch | VM Manager](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/vm-manager/docs/patch) · [About VM Manager | Compute Engine](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/vm-manager)

questions.domain: Securing communications and establishing boundary protection
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An organization’s security and risk-management teams are concerned about the boundaries between their responsibilities and Google’s responsibilities for certain production workloads running in Google Cloud. They mostly run workloads with Google Cloud platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) offerings, primarily App Engine.  
  
Which technology-stack area should be their primary responsibility when using App Engine?

options.text: Configuring and monitoring VPC Flow Logs
Defending against XSS and SQLi attacks
Managing the latest updates and security patches for the Guest OS
Encrypting all stored data

questions.explanation:
App Engine is a PaaS service: Google manages more of the underlying platform, while the customer shares responsibility for application-level controls and remains responsible for client protection. Defending the application against cross-site scripting (XSS) and SQL injection (SQLi) is therefore a customer responsibility.

**Learn more:** [Shared responsibilities and shared fate on Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/security/shared-responsibility-shared-fate)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization's Customers must scan and upload their contract and driver license to a web portal in Cloud Storage. You must remove all personally identifiable information (PII) from files older than 12 months. You must also archive the anonymized files for retention purposes.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Set a time to live (TTL) of 12 months for the files in the Cloud Storage bucket that removes PII and moves the files to the archive storage class.
Create a Cloud Data loss Prevention (DLP) inspection job that de-identifies PII in files created more than 12 months ago and archives them to another Cloud Storage bucket. Delete the original files.
Configure the Autoclass feature of the Cloud Storage bucket to de-identify PII. Archive the files that are older than 12 months. Delete the original files.
Schedule a Cloud Key Management Service (KMS) rotation period of 12 months for the encryption keys of the Cloud Storage files containing PII to de-identify them. Delete the original keys.

questions.explanation:
Sensitive Data Protection can inspect files in Cloud Storage for PII and create de-identified copies in a separate Cloud Storage bucket. The original files are not modified by that operation, so deleting them after the de-identified copies are archived removes the retained PII while preserving anonymized records for retention. Cloud Storage lifecycle rules and Autoclass only manage object age and storage classes; they do not inspect or redact file contents. KMS key rotation does not de-identify data.

**Learn more:** [De-identification of sensitive Cloud Storage data](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/concepts-deidentify-storage) · [Create de-identified copies of data stored in Cloud Storage using the API](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/deidentify-storage)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team uses a service account to authenticate data transfers from a given Compute Engine virtual machine instance to a specified Cloud Storage bucket. An engineer accidentally deletes the service account, breaking application functionality. You want to restore the application as quickly as possible without compromising security.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Temporarily disable authentication on the Cloud Storage bucket.
Use the undelete command to recover the deleted service account.
Create a new service account with the same name as the deleted service account.
Update the permissions of another existing service account and supply those credentials to the applications.

questions.explanation:
Undeleting the service account restores its original identity and retained IAM role bindings when it is still within the 30-day recovery window. This returns the Compute Engine workload's authorized access without weakening Cloud Storage authentication or substituting a different principal with newly altered permissions.

**Learn more:** [Delete and undelete service accounts](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/service-accounts-delete-undelete)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage data in your organization’s Cloud Storage buckets and are required to retain objects. To reduce storage costs, you must automatically downgrade the storage class of objects older than 365 days to Coldline storage. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Asset Inventory to generate a report of the configuration of all storage buckets. Examine the Lifecycle management policy settings and ensure that they are set correctly.
Set up a CloudRun Job with Cloud Scheduler to execute a script that searches for and removes flies older than 365 days from your Cloud Storage.
Enable the Autoclass feature to manage all aspects of bucket storage classes.
Define a lifecycle policy JSON with an action on SetStorageClass to COLDLINE with an age condition of 365 and matchStorageClass STANDARD.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Storage lifecycle management can automatically transition objects when they meet specified conditions. A lifecycle rule with `SetStorageClass` set to `COLDLINE`, an `age` condition of `365`, and `matchesStorageClass` set to `STANDARD` moves eligible Standard objects to Coldline without deleting them.

**Learn more:** [Object Lifecycle Management | Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/lifecycle) · [Configuration examples for Object Lifecycle Management | Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/lifecycle-configurations)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are responsible for establishing a new Google Cloud organization for your company. Which two actions should you take when creating the super administrator accounts? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create an access level in the Google Admin console to prevent super admin from logging in to Google Cloud.
Disable any Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles for super admin at the organization level in the Google Cloud Console.
Use a physical token to secure the super admin credentials with multi-factor authentication (MFA).
Use a private connection to create the super admin accounts to avoid sending your credentials over the Internet.
Provide non-privileged identities to the super admin users for their day-to-day activities.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud recommends enforcing two-step verification for super-admin accounts with a security key or other physical authentication device. It also recommends giving each administrator a separate, less-privileged identity for routine work and using the dedicated super-admin identity only when elevated privileges are required.

**Learn more:** [Super administrator account best practices](https://docs.cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/super-admin-best-practices?hl=en) · [Best practices for federating Google Cloud with an external identity provider](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/identity/best-practices-for-federating)

options.text: Use VPC Service Controls to create perimeters around each business unit's project.
Organize projects in folders, and assign permissions to Google groups at the folder level.
Group business units based on Organization Units (OUs) and manage permissions based on OUs
Create a project naming convention, and use Google's IAM Conditions to manage access based on the prefix of project names.
Use Google Cloud Directory Sync to synchronize users and group memberships in Cloud Identity.

questions.explanation:
Folders create administrative boundaries in the Google Cloud resource hierarchy, and IAM roles granted to Google groups at a folder are inherited by its projects. This enables business-unit-specific, scalable access control through group membership. Google Cloud Directory Sync synchronizes users and group memberships from an on-premises directory to Cloud Identity, so directory membership changes revoke inherited access for transfers and departing users.

**Learn more:** [Access control for folders with IAM](https://cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/access-control-folders) · [Create and manage Google groups in the Google Cloud console](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/groups-in-cloud-console)

A customer plans to migrate sensitive workloads to a Compute Engine-based cluster that uses Managed Instance Groups (MIGs). The jobs are bursty and need to finish quickly. The customer requires control over the key lifecycle.  
  
Which boot disk encryption solution should be used on the cluster to satisfy these requirements?

options.text: Customer-supplied encryption keys (CSEK)
Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) using Cloud Key Management Service (KMS)
Encryption by default
Pre-encrypting files before transferring to Google Cloud Platform (GCP) for analysis

questions.explanation:
Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) in Cloud KMS provide control over key protection level, location, rotation schedule, usage, access permissions, auditing, and key lifecycle. They can encrypt Compute Engine persistent disks, including boot disks, while supporting automated Managed Instance Group scaling without managing and supplying raw keys for each instance operation.

**Learn more:** [About disk encryption](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/disks/disk-encryption) · [Protect resources with Cloud KMS keys](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/disks/customer-managed-encryption)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization formerly stored files in Cloud Storage using Google Managed Encryption Keys (GMEK), but has recently changed its internal policy to require Customer Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK). You need to re-encrypt the files quickly and efficiently at minimal cost.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Reupload the files to the same Cloud Storage bucket specifying a key file by using gsutil.
Encrypt the files locally, and then use gsutil to upload the files to a new bucket.
Copy the files to a new bucket with CMEK enabled in a secondary region.
Change the encryption type on the bucket to CMEK, and rewrite the objects.

questions.explanation:
A bucket’s default CMEK applies when objects are written, but changing it does not retroactively encrypt existing objects with that key. Existing objects must be rewritten to apply CMEK; rewriting them in the same bucket after setting its default CMEK avoids unnecessary local transfers and a second bucket.

**Learn more:** [Customer-managed encryption keys | Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/encryption/customer-managed-keys) · [Use customer-managed encryption keys | Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/encryption/using-customer-managed-keys)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your DevOps team uses Packer to create Compute Engine images through this process:  
  
1. Create a temporary Compute Engine VM.  
2. Copy a binary from a Cloud Storage bucket to the VM file system.  
3. Update the VM package manager.  
4. Install external internet packages on the VM.  
  
Your security team has just enabled the organizational policy `constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess` to limit the use of public IP addresses on VMs. In response, your DevOps team updated its scripts to remove public IP addresses from the Compute Engine VMs; however, the build pipeline now fails because of connectivity problems.  
  
What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Provision an HTTP load balancer with the VM in an unmanaged instance group to allow inbound connections from the internet to your VM.
Provision a Cloud NAT instance in the same VPC and region as the Compute Engine VM.
Enable Private Google Access on the subnet that the Compute Engine VM is deployed within.
Update the VPC routes to allow traffic to and from the internet.
Provision a Cloud VPN tunnel in the same VPC and region as the Compute Engine VM.

questions.explanation:
Cloud NAT provides outbound internet access for Compute Engine VMs that have no external IP address, allowing the VM to retrieve packages from internet repositories. Private Google Access, enabled on the VM subnet, permits an internal-IP-only VM to access Google APIs and services, including Cloud Storage.

**Learn more:** [Cloud NAT overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/nat/docs/overview) · [Configure Private Google Access](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/configure-private-google-access)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company operates redundant mail servers across different Google Cloud Platform regions and needs to direct customers to the nearest mail server according to location.  
  
How should the company do this?

options.text: Configure TCP Proxy Load Balancing as a global load balancing service listening on port 995.
Create a Network Load Balancer to listen on TCP port 995 with a forwarding rule to forward traffic based on location.
Use Cross-Region Load Balancing with an HTTP(S) load balancer to route traffic to the nearest region.
Use Cloud CDN to route the mail traffic to the closest origin mail server based on client IP address.

questions.explanation:
A global TCP Proxy Load Balancer supports non-HTTP TCP services on a single global IP address. With globally distributed front ends and backends in multiple regions, it directs new connections toward healthy backends in the region closest to the user. TCP port 995 can be configured as the listener port for this service.

**Learn more:** [External proxy Network Load Balancer overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/tcp)

questions.question:
A customer requires an alternative to keeping plain-text secrets in their source-code management (SCM) system.  
  
How should the customer accomplish this by using Google Cloud Platform?

options.text: Use Cloud Source Repositories, and store secrets in Cloud SQL.
Encrypt the secrets with a Customer-Managed Encryption Key (CMEK), and store them in Cloud Storage.
Run the Cloud Data Loss Prevention API to scan the secrets, and store them in Cloud SQL.
Deploy the SCM to a Compute Engine VM with local SSDs, and enable preemptible VMs.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Storage supports customer-managed encryption keys (CMEKs) from Cloud KMS, allowing secret data to be stored outside the source repository while the customer controls key use, rotation, permissions, and lifecycle.\
\
**Learn more:** [Customer-managed encryption keys — Cloud Storage](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/encryption/customer-managed-keys)

questions.question:
A customer requires an alternative to keeping plain-text secrets in their source-code management (SCM) system.  
  
How should the customer accomplish this by using Google Cloud Platform?

options.text: Create an Alerting Policy in Stackdriver using a Process Health condition, checking that the number of executions of the script remains below the desired threshold. Enable notifications.
Create an Alerting Policy in Stackdriver using the CPU usage metric. Set the threshold to 80% to be notified when the CPU usage goes above this 80%.
Log every execution of the script to Stackdriver Logging. Create a User-defined metric in Stackdriver Logging on the logs, and create a Stackdriver Dashboard displaying the metric.
Log every execution of the script to Stackdriver Logging. Configure BigQuery as a log sink, and create a BigQuery scheduled query to count the number of executions in a specific timeframe.

questions.explanation:
A process-health alerting policy can monitor the number of VM processes whose invocation command matches the script and notify when that number exceeds the permitted threshold. This directly detects the repeated script executions that cause the instance crash. CPU utilization is not a reliable indicator of this event, and collecting logs, displaying a dashboard, or running a BigQuery query alone does not notify responders. [Monitor count of processes on a VM](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/alerts/monitor-process-count?hl=en)

**Learn more:** [Monitor count of processes on a VM](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/alerts/monitor-process-count?hl=en) · [Alerting overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/alerts)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization runs an application on Cloud Run. You need to control access to the application with Cloud Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) and meet these requirements:  
  
- Only users in the AppDev group can access it.  
- Access must be limited to internal network IP addresses.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Deploy a VPN gateway and instruct the AppDev group to connect to the company network before accessing the application.
Create an access level that includes conditions for internal IP address ranges and AppDev groups. Apply this access level to the application's IAP policy.
Configure firewall rules to limit access to IAP based on the AppDev group and source IP addresses.
Configure IAP to enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA) for all users and use network intrusion detection systems (NIDS) to block unauthorized access attempts.

questions.explanation:
IAP policies can grant access to a Google group, while Context-Aware Access access levels can restrict access by IP address. Binding the AppDev group to the IAP-protected application with an access level that permits only the internal IP ranges enforces both identity-based and network-context requirements.

**Learn more:** [Setting up context-aware access with Identity-Aware Proxy](https://cloud.google.com/iap/docs/cloud-iap-context-aware-access-howto) · [Configure IAP for Cloud Run](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/securing/identity-aware-proxy-cloud-run)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company requires the security and network engineering teams to detect all network anomalies within and across VPCs, internal VM-to-VM traffic, traffic between internet endpoints and VMs, and traffic from VMs to Google Cloud services in production. Which method should be used?

options.text: Define an organization policy constraint.
Configure packet mirroring policies.
Enable VPC Flow Logs on the subnet.
Monitor and analyze Cloud Audit Logs.

questions.explanation:
VPC Flow Logs provides network-flow telemetry for VM traffic in a subnet, including flows within Google Cloud and between Google Cloud and other networks. Its records can include VPC, VM, internet-routing, and Google-service metadata, enabling security and network teams to analyze anomalous traffic patterns across the required communication paths.

**Learn more:** [VPC Flow Logs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/flow-logs) · [About VPC Flow Logs records](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/about-flow-logs-records)

questions.domain: Securing communications and establishing boundary protection
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A customer runs an analytics workload on Compute Engine that needs restricted internet access.  
  
Your team created an egress firewall rule that denies (priority 1000) all traffic to the internet. The Compute Engine instances now must access the public repository to obtain security updates.  
  
What should your team do?

options.text: Create an egress firewall rule to allow traffic to the CIDR range of the repository with a priority greater than 1000.
Create an egress firewall rule to allow traffic to the CIDR range of the repository with a priority less than 1000.
Create an egress firewall rule to allow traffic to the hostname of the repository with a priority greater than 1000.
Create an egress firewall rule to allow traffic to the hostname of the repository with a priority less than 1000.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud evaluates applicable VPC firewall rules by priority, where a lower numeric value has higher priority. A narrowly scoped egress allow rule for the repository’s destination CIDR range with a priority below 1000 overrides the broader deny-all-internet rule, while other internet egress remains denied.

**Learn more:** [VPC firewall rules](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewalls) · [Use VPC firewall rules](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/using-firewalls)

questions.domain: Securing communications and establishing boundary protection
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization runs a hybrid cloud environment and has recently deployed a private Artifact Registry repository in Google Cloud. On-premises developers are unable to resolve the Artifact Registry hostname, so they cannot push or pull artifacts. You have confirmed the following:  
  
- Connectivity to Google Cloud is established through Cloud VPN or Cloud Interconnect.  
- No custom DNS configuration exists on-premises.  
- The on-premises network has no route to the internet.  
  
You need to determine the cause and allow the developers to push and pull artifacts. What is likely causing the issue, and what should you do to resolve it?

options.text: On-premises DNS servers lack the necessary records to resolve private Google API domains. Create DNS records for restricted.googleapis.com or private.googleapis.com pointing to Google's published IP ranges.
Developers must be granted the artifactregistry.writer IAM role. Grant the relevant developer group this role.
Private Google Access is not enabled for the subnet hosting the Artifact Registry. Enable Private Google Access for the appropriate subnet.
Artifact Registry requires external HTTP/HTTPS access. Create a new firewall rule allowing ingress traffic on ports 80 and 443 from the developer's IP ranges.

questions.explanation:
Private Google Access for on-premises hosts requires DNS zones and records that resolve the required Google service domains to the VIP addresses for `private.googleapis.com` or `restricted.googleapis.com`. Without that private DNS configuration, on-premises clients cannot resolve the private Artifact Registry access endpoint. Private Google Access does not need to be enabled on a VPC subnet for on-premises hosts using Cloud VPN or Cloud Interconnect.

**Learn more:** [Configure Private Google Access for on-premises hosts](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/configure-private-google-access-hybrid) · [Private Google Access for on-premises hosts](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/private-google-access-hybrid)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],After a security vulnerability assessment, you discovered that cloud administrators keep Google Cloud CLI sessions open for days. To reduce the risk of attackers exploiting these open sessions, you need to configure the sessions for the minimum duration.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Set the session duration for the Google session control to one hour.
Set the reauthentication frequency for the Google Cloud Session Control to one hour.
Set the organization policy constraint constraints/iam.allowServiceAccountCredentialLifetimeExtension to one hour.
Set the organization policy constraint constraints/iam.serviceAccountKeyExpiryHours to one hour and inheritFromParent to false.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Session Control applies to Google Cloud CLI access and uses the reauthentication frequency to limit how long a user can access Google Cloud without authenticating again. One hour is the minimum supported session length, so setting the Google Cloud Session Control reauthentication frequency to one hour limits these interactive CLI sessions accordingly.

**Learn more:** [Configure session controls for reauthentication](https://cloud.google.com/access-context-manager/docs/session-controls-for-reauthentication) · [Authenticate for the gcloud CLI](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/docs/authenticate)

questions.question: Which international compliance standard offers guidance on information security controls applicable to providing and using cloud services?
questions.explanation:
ISO/IEC 27017 provides cloud-specific information security control guidance, including additional implementation guidance and controls for cloud service providers and cloud service customers.\
\
**Learn more:** [ISO/IEC 27017:2015 — Security techniques: Code of practice for information security controls for cloud services](https://www.iso.org/standard/43757.html)

questions.question: Which international compliance standard offers guidance on information security controls applicable to providing and using cloud services?

options.text: Configure a Cloud NAT gateway to enable internet access from the developer instance subnet.
Ensure that the developers have restarted their instance and HTTP service is enabled.
Ensure that the developers have explicitly configured the proxy address on their instance.
Configure a firewall rule to allow HTTP/S from the developer instance.

questions.explanation:
In explicit proxy routing mode, client instances must be explicitly configured to direct their HTTP/S requests to the Secure Web Proxy address and port. Without that client-side proxy configuration, developer traffic does not traverse the Secure Web Proxy and its allowed-URL policy.

**Learn more:** [Quickstart: Deploy a Secure Web Proxy instance](https://cloud.google.com/secure-web-proxy/docs/quickstart) · [Secure Web Proxy overview](https://cloud.google.com/secure-web-proxy/docs/overview)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You administer the security logs in your cloud environment. You have set up a continuous export of security logs to Cloud Storage buckets for long-term retention. You need to enable auditors to analyze the logs exported to Cloud Storage. The solution must be cost-effective and fast to implement.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use a VM instance to download the data from Cloud Storage. Provide the auditors access to the VM and allow them to install their preferred analytics toolset.
Use the data in the Cloud Storage bucket as an external table in BigQuery. Provide the auditors access to the BigQuery dataset.
Use Dataflow to import the data from Cloud Storage into Elasticsearch. Provide the auditors with access to Elasticsearch.
Use a Cloud Run job to import the log data from Cloud Storage to Cloud Logging. Provide the auditors access through Log Analytics.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery external tables let users query supported data stored in Cloud Storage without first loading or copying it into another analytics system. This avoids managing a VM or implementing a Dataflow or Cloud Run ingestion pipeline, while IAM permissions can give auditors access to query the external table and its underlying Cloud Storage data.

**Learn more:** [Create Cloud Storage external tables](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/external-data-cloud-storage) · [Query Cloud Storage data in external tables](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/query-cloud-storage-data)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization is developing a real-time recommendation engine that uses ML models to process live user-activity data stored in BigQuery and Cloud Storage. Each newly developed model is stored in Artifact Registry. The system deploys models to Google Kubernetes Engine and uses Pub/Sub for message queues. Recent industry reports describe attacks that exploit ML model supply chains.  
  
You need to strengthen security in this serverless architecture, particularly against risks in the development and deployment pipeline. What should you do?

options.text: Enable container image vulnerability scanning during development and pre-deployment. Enforce Binary Authorization on images deployed from Artifact Registry to your continuous integration and continuous deployment (CVCD) pipeline.

Thoroughly sanitize all training data prior to model development to reduce risk of poisoning attacks. Use IAM for authorization, and apply role-based restrictions to code repositories and cloud services.

Limit external libraries and dependencies that are used for the ML models as much as possible. Continuously rotate encryption keys that are used to access the user data from BigQuery and Cloud Storage.
Develop strict firewall rules to limit external traffic to Cloud Run instances. Integrate intrusion detection systems (IDS) for real-time anomaly detection on Pub/Sub message flows.

questions.explanation:
Container image vulnerability scanning detects known vulnerabilities before deployment, and Binary Authorization enforces deploy-time policy for GKE workloads. It can require trusted attestations for images stored in Artifact Registry, preventing unapproved or altered artifacts from being deployed and thereby protecting the software and model supply chain.

**Learn more:** [Binary Authorization overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/overview) · [Create a Binary Authorization attestation in a Cloud Build pipeline](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/cloud-build)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization depends heavily on virtual machines (VMs) in Compute Engine. Because the team and resource demands are growing, VM sprawl is becoming a problem. Maintaining consistent security hardening and prompt package updates is increasingly difficult. You need to centralize VM image management and automate enforcement of security baselines across the virtual machine lifecycle. What should you do?

options.text: Use VM Manager to automatically distribute and apply patches to YMs across your projects. Integrate VM Manager with hardened, organization-standard VM images stored in a central repository.

Configure the sole-tenancy feature in Compute Engine for all projects. Set up custom organization policies in Policy Controller to restrict the operating systems and image sources that teams are allowed to use.

Create a Cloud Build trigger to build a pipeline that generates hardened VM images. Run vulnerability scans in the pipeline, and store images with passing scans in a registry. Use instance templates pointing to this registry.
Activate Security Command Center Enterprise. Use VM discovery and posture management features to monitor hardening state and trigger automatic responses upon detection of issues.

questions.explanation:
VM Manager provides centralized, scheduled patch deployment for Compute Engine VM fleets. Its OS policies define desired operating-system resources and are periodically checked and enforced on targeted VMs, maintaining configuration consistency and reporting compliance. Organization-standard hardened images in a central image project provide a consistent starting point for newly created VMs, while VM Manager maintains the baseline and updates after deployment.

**Learn more:** [About VM Manager](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/vm-manager) · [About OS policies](https://cloud.google.com/compute/vm-manager/docs/os-policies)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are your company's security administrator. You have 3,000 objects in your Cloud Storage bucket, and you do not want to manage access to every object individually.  
  
You also do not want an object's uploader to always have full control of that object. However, you want to use Cloud Audit Logs to manage access to your bucket.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Set up an ACL with OWNER permission to a scope of allUsers.
Set up an ACL with READER permission to a scope of allUsers.
Set up a default bucket ACL and manage access for users using IAM.
Set up Uniform bucket-level access on the Cloud Storage bucket and manage access for users using IAM.

questions.explanation:
Uniform bucket-level access disables Cloud Storage ACLs and grants access to the bucket and all its objects exclusively through bucket-level IAM roles. This avoids individual object access management and prevents uploader-specific object ACL ownership from controlling access. Cloud Audit Logs records relevant access and administrative activity; IAM is the authorization mechanism.

**Learn more:** [Uniform bucket-level access | Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/uniform-bucket-level-access) · [Cloud Audit Logs with Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/audit-logging)

questions.domain: Securing communications and establishing boundary protection
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company runs a critical web application on Google Cloud. The application is seeing a growing number of sophisticated Layer 7 attacks, including cross-site scripting (XSS) and SQL injection attempts. You must protect the application from these attacks while minimizing effects on legitimate traffic and maintaining high availability. What should you do?

options.text: Implement a load balancer in front of the web application instances, and enable Adaptive Protection and throttling to mitigate the occurrence of these malicious requests.
Configure Cloud Next Generation Firewall to block known malicious IP addresses targeting /32 addresses.
Enable Google Cloud Armor’s pre-configured WAF rules for OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities at the backend service.
Configure a Cloud Armor security policy with customized and pre-configured WAF rules for OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities at the load balancer.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Armor preconfigured WAF rules use OWASP Core Rule Set signatures, including signatures for XSS and SQL injection. A Cloud Armor security policy is attached to the Application Load Balancer’s backend service, where the rules can be tuned to reduce false positives while filtering malicious Layer 7 requests before they reach the application.

**Learn more:** [Google Cloud Armor preconfigured WAF rules overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/waf-rules) · [Create and manage Google Cloud Armor security policies](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/configure-security-policies)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization is migrating virtual machines (VMs) to Google Cloud. You need to ensure that operating system images used throughout your projects are trusted and satisfy your security requirements.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Implement an organization policy to enforce that boot disks can only be created from images that come from the trusted image project.
Implement an organization policy constraint that enables the Shielded VM service on all projects to enforce the trusted image repository usage.
Create a Cloud Function that is automatically triggered when a new virtual machine is created from the trusted image repository. Verify that the image is not deprecated.
Automate a security scanner that verifies that no common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVEs) are present in your trusted image repository.

questions.explanation:
The `compute.trustedImageProjects` organization policy constraint restricts creation of boot disks to images from specified, approved image projects. Configuring it to allow only the trusted image project enforces trusted OS-image use across the affected projects.

**Learn more:** [Set up trusted image policies](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/images/restricting-image-access)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Employees at your company use their own computers to access your organization's Google Cloud console. You must ensure that users can access the Google Cloud console only from corporate-issued devices and confirm that they hold a valid enterprise certificate.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Implement an Access Policy in BeyondCorp Enterprise to verify the device certificate. Create an access binding with the access policy just created.
Implement a VPC firewall policy. Activate packet inspection and create an allow rule to validate and verify the device certificate.
Implement an organization policy to verify the certificate from the access context.
Implement an Identity and Access Management (IAM) conditional policy to verify the device certificate.

questions.explanation:
BeyondCorp Enterprise certificate-based access can require a verified X.509 device certificate that matches an existing trusted device. The certificate requirement is expressed in an Access Context Manager access level and enforced for the relevant users and Google Cloud console through an access binding.

**Learn more:** [Define access policies with access levels](https://cloud.google.com/beyondcorp-enterprise/docs/define-access-policies) · [Apply certificate-based access for user groups](https://cloud.google.com/beyondcorp-enterprise/docs/enable-cba-user-groups)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You administer an analytical data warehouse in BigQuery for your organization. You need to retain data for every customer in a shared table while restricting query access according to row- and column-level permissions. Non-query operations must not be supported.  
  
What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create row-level access policies to restrict the result data when you run queries with the filter expression set to TRUE.
Configure column-level encryption by using Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) functions with Cloud Key Management Service (KMS) to control access to columns at query runtime.
Create row-level access policies to restrict the result data when you run queries with the filter expression set to FALSE.
Configure dynamic data masking rules to control access to columns at query runtime.
Create column-level policy tags to control access to columns at query runtime.

questions.explanation:
Column-level security in BigQuery is implemented with policy tags, so E is required. For rows, a row access policy with the filter expression set to TRUE grants full access to all rows and is precisely what enables non-query operations such as DML, copy, export, and tabledata.list; since the requirement is that non-query operations must NOT be supported, you must avoid the TRUE full-access grant, making C (filter FALSE) correct and A (filter TRUE) wrong. Applying row-level access policies to the table also inherently blocks the unsupported non-query operations. Together, C and E restrict query access by row and column while ensuring non-query operations remain unsupported.

**Learn more:** [Row-level security with other features](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/using-row-level-security-with-features) · [Column-level access control](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/column-level-security-intro)

questions.question:
A large financial institution is migrating its Big Data analytics to Google Cloud Platform. It wants maximum control over the encryption process for data stored at rest in BigQuery.  
  
Which technique should the institution use?

options.text: Use Cloud Storage as a federated Data Source.
Use a Cloud Hardware Security Module (Cloud HSM).
Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK).
Customer-supplied encryption keys (CSEK).

questions.explanation:
Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) let an organization control the Cloud KMS key that BigQuery uses to protect data at rest, including key access, rotation, and the ability to disable or destroy the key. BigQuery supports CMEK for this purpose.\
\
**Learn more:** [Customer-managed Cloud KMS keys | BigQuery](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/customer-managed-encryption)

questions.question:
A large financial institution is migrating its Big Data analytics to Google Cloud Platform. It wants maximum control over the encryption process for data stored at rest in BigQuery.  
  
Which technique should the institution use?

options.text: Set appropriate rowsLimit value on BigQuery data hosted outside the US and set appropriate bytesLimitPerFile value on multiregional Cloud Storage buckets.
Set appropriate rowsLimit value on BigQuery data hosted outside the US, and minimize transformation units on multiregional Cloud Storage buckets.
Use rowsLimit and bytesLimitPerFile to sample data and use CloudStorageRegexFileSet to limit scans.
Use FindingLimits and TimespanContfig to sample data and minimize transformation units.

questions.explanation:
Sensitive Data Protection storage inspection is billed by the bytes inspected. `rowsLimit` samples BigQuery rows, `bytesLimitPerFile` restricts the amount inspected from each Cloud Storage file, and `CloudStorageRegexFileSet` uses regular-expression filters to include or exclude files and folders, reducing the scan scope and associated cost.

**Learn more:** [Keeping costs under control | Sensitive Data Protection](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/best-practices-costs) · [Pricing | Sensitive Data Protection](https://cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/pricing)

questions.question:
A manager needs to begin retaining security event logs for 2 years while keeping costs to a minimum. You create a filter to select the relevant log entries.  
  
Where should the logs be exported?

options.text: BigQuery datasets
Cloud Storage buckets
StackDriver logging
Cloud Pub/Sub topics

questions.explanation:
Cloud Storage buckets are the appropriate destination for long-term log retention at minimized cost. Cloud Logging identifies Cloud Storage as the sink destination for long-term storage; its storage classes and lifecycle controls support economical retention over a two-year period. BigQuery is primarily suited to analytics, and Pub/Sub is intended for streaming logs to downstream integrations.\
\
**Learn more:** [Route logs to supported destinations](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/configure_export_v2) · [Cloud Storage classes](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/storage-classes)

questions.domain: Securing communications and establishing boundary protection

options.text: Create a Cloud Build pipeline that will monitor changes to your container templates in a Cloud Source Repositories repository. Add a step to analyze Container Analysis results before allowing the build to continue.
Use a Cloud Function triggered by log events in Google Cloud's operations suite to automatically scan your container images in Container Registry.
Use a cron job on a Compute Engine instance to scan your existing repositories for known vulnerabilities and raise an alert if a non-compliant container image is found.
Deploy Jenkins on GKE and configure a CI/CD pipeline to deploy your containers to Container Registry. Add a step to validate your container images before deploying your container to the cluster.

In your CI/CD pipeline, add an attestation on your container image when no vulnerabilities have been found. Use a Binary Authorization policy to block deployments of containers with no attestation in your cluster.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Build can evaluate Container Analysis vulnerability findings as part of the managed CI/CD workflow. After an image has passed the vulnerability check, the pipeline can create an attestation for its immutable image digest. A Binary Authorization policy on GKE can require that attestation and enforce deployment-time blocking for images that do not have it. [Google Cloud: Create a Binary Authorization attestation in a Cloud Build pipeline](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/cloud-build) and [Binary Authorization overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/overview).

**Learn more:** [Create a Binary Authorization attestation in a Cloud Build pipeline](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/cloud-build) · [Binary Authorization overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/overview)

Your organization’s Google Cloud VMs are deployed using an instance template that assigns them public IP addresses to host web services for external users. The VMs are located in a service project attached to a host (VPC) project that contains one custom Shared VPC for the VMs. You must reduce the VMs’ internet exposure while still serving external users. You have already recreated the instance template without a public-IP-address configuration to launch the managed instance group (MIG). What should you do?

options.text: Deploy a Cloud NAT Gateway in the service project for the MIG.
Deploy a Cloud NAT Gateway in the host (VPC) project for the MIG.
Deploy an external HTTP(S) load balancer in the service project with the MIG as a backend.
Deploy an external HTTP(S) load balancer in the host (VPC) project with the MIG as a backend.

questions.explanation:
Cloud NAT provides only outbound connectivity for VMs that lack external IP addresses, so it cannot publish web services to internet clients. An external HTTP(S) load balancer provides the public endpoint and routes requests to the MIG’s internal VM addresses. For a typical Shared VPC deployment with backend instances in a service project, Google Cloud places the load-balancer components in that same service project.

**Learn more:** [External Application Load Balancer overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/https) · [Shared VPC overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/shared-vpc)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A website design company recently moved all customer sites to App Engine. Some sites remain in development and must be visible only to customers and company employees, regardless of their location.  
  
Which solution restricts access to the in-progress sites?

options.text: Upload an .htaccess file containing the customer and employee user accounts to App Engine.
Create an App Engine firewall rule that allows access from the customer and employee networks and denies all other traffic.
Enable Cloud Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP), and allow access to a Google Group that contains the customer and employee user accounts.
Use Cloud VPN to create a VPN connection between the relevant on-premises networks and the company's GCP Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network.

questions.explanation:
Identity-Aware Proxy secures App Engine applications with identity-based authentication and IAM authorization. Granting the IAP-secured Web App User role to a Google Group permits only the group’s customer and employee members to access the protected sites from any location, without relying on source networks or a VPN.

**Learn more:** [Enabling IAP for App Engine](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iap/docs/enabling-app-engine) · [Manage access to IAP-secured resources](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iap/docs/managing-access)

questions.domain: Securing communications and establishing boundary protection
questions.question: Which two implied firewall rules exist on a VPC network? (Choose two.)

options.text: A rule that allows all outbound connections
A rule that denies all inbound connections
A rule that blocks all inbound port 25 connections
A rule that blocks all outbound connections
A rule that allows all inbound port 80 connections

questions.explanation:
Every Google Cloud VPC network has an implied deny-ingress firewall rule that blocks all incoming connections and an implied allow-egress firewall rule that permits all outgoing connections, unless higher-priority rules override them.\
\
**Learn more:** [VPC firewall rules](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewalls) · [Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/overview)

questions.question: Which two implied firewall rules exist on a VPC network? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use Cloud Storage with customer-supplied encryption keys (CSEK), VPC Service Controls for network isolation, and Cloud DLP for data inspection.
Use Cloud Storage with customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK), Cloud DLP for data classification, and Secret Manager for storing API access tokens.
Use Cloud Storage with client-side encryption, Cloud KMS for key management, and Cloud HSM for cryptographic operations.
Use Cloud Storage with server-side encryption, BigQuery with column-level encryption, and IAM roles for access control.

questions.explanation:
Client-side encryption protects data before it is sent to Cloud Storage and gives the customer full control of encryption and decryption. Cloud KMS centrally manages the keys, while Cloud HSM performs cryptographic operations with HSM-protected keys, providing hardware-backed protection for highly sensitive data.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Storage data encryption options](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/encryption) · [Cloud HSM documentation](https://cloud.google.com/kms/docs/hsm)

A company operates in a regulated industry requiring low-overhead encryption over private connectivity from on-premises data centers to Google Cloud. Connectivity must be established with high availability across multiple regions. What should be done?

options.text: Set up two pairs of HA VPNs using IPSec from the data centers in multiple regions.
Set up pairs of Cloud Interconnect connections to your data centers in multiple regions, and employ MACSec encryption.
Set up L2TP encryption over pairs of dedicated Cloud Interconnect connections from the data centers in multiple regions.
Set up IPSec encryption over Partner Interconnect connections from your data centers in multiple regions.

questions.explanation:
Dedicated Cloud Interconnect provides private connectivity from on-premises networks to Google Cloud, and MACsec encrypts traffic between the on-premises router and Google edge routers. A multi-region production topology uses redundant pairs of Cloud Interconnect connections across regions to provide high availability. MACsec supplies link-layer encryption without the tunnel encapsulation overhead of IPsec.

**Learn more:** [MACsec for Cloud Interconnect overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/concepts/macsec-overview) · [Topology for production-level applications overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/tutorials/production-level-overview)

An organization has acquired a new workload. The Web and Application (App) servers will run on Compute Engine in a newly created custom VPC. You are responsible for configuring a secure network-communication solution that meets these requirements:  
  
- Allow communication only between the Web and App tiers.  
- Enforce consistent network security as the Web and App tiers autoscale.  
- Prevent Compute Engine Instance Admins from changing network traffic.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: 1. Configure all running Web and App servers with respective network tags. 2. Create an allow VPC firewall rule that specifies the target/source with respective network tags.
1. Configure all running Web and App servers with respective service accounts. 2. Create an allow VPC firewall rule that specifies the target/source with respective service accounts.

1. Re-deploy the Web and App servers with instance templates configured with respective network tags. 2. Create an allow VPC firewall rule that specifies the target/source with respective network tags.

1. Re-deploy the Web and App servers with instance templates configured with respective service accounts. 2. Create an allow VPC firewall rule that specifies the target/source with respective service accounts.

questions.explanation:
VPC firewall rules can use source and target service accounts to allow traffic only between the Web and App VM groups. Configuring the distinct service accounts in their instance templates ensures that new autoscaled instances automatically receive the correct firewall identity. Network tags are not suitable for strict control because a principal with the Compute Engine Instance Admin role can edit an instance's tags; attaching or using a service account is controlled separately through IAM, including the Service Account User role.

**Learn more:** [VPC firewall rules — Filter by service account versus network tag](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewalls) · [Compute Engine access control overview](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/access)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An organization requires complete control over the keys used to encrypt data at rest in its Google Cloud environments. The keys must be generated and stored outside Google, while integrating with numerous Google services, including BigQuery.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use customer-supplied encryption keys (CSEK) with keys generated on trusted external systems. Provide the raw CSEK as part of the API call.

Create a KMS key that is stored on a Google managed FIPS 140-2 level 3 Hardware Security Module (HSM). Manage the Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions settings, and set up the key rotation period.
Use Cloud External Key Management (EKM) that integrates with an external Hardware Security Module (HSM) system from supported vendors.
Create a Cloud Key Management Service (KMS) key with imported key material. Wrap the key for protection during import. Import the key generated on a trusted system in Cloud KMS.

questions.explanation:
Cloud External Key Manager (Cloud EKM) lets Google Cloud services use keys that remain managed in a supported external key-management system, including an external HSM. The external key material is never stored in or sent to Google, and BigQuery is among the services that support Cloud EKM keys.

**Learn more:** [Cloud External Key Manager overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kms/docs/ekm)

questions.question: You want to stop users from inadvertently deleting a Shared VPC host project. Which organization-level policy constraint should you enable?

options.text: compute.restrictSharedVpcHostProjects
compute.restrictXpnProjectLienRemoval
compute.restrictSharedVpcSubnetworks
compute.sharedReservationsOwnerProjects

questions.explanation:
Enforcing `compute.restrictXpnProjectLienRemoval` restricts removal of the Shared VPC host-project lien to principals with the required organization-level permission, preventing a project owner from accidentally deleting the host project. [Google Cloud: Provision Shared VPC](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/provisioning-shared-vpc)\
\
**Learn more:** [Provision Shared VPC | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/provisioning-shared-vpc) · [Organization policies for Compute Engine | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/access/organization-policies)

questions.question: You want to stop users from inadvertently deleting a Shared VPC host project. Which organization-level policy constraint should you enable?

options.text: Change the configuration of the relevant groups in the Google Workspace Admin console to prevent external users from being added to the group.
Set an Identity and Access Management (IAM) policy that includes a condition that restricts group membership to user principals that belong to your organization.
Define an Identity and Access Management (IAM) deny policy that denies the assignment of principals that are outside your organization to the groups in scope.
Export the Cloud Identity logs to BigQuery. Configure an alert for external members added to groups. Have the alert trigger a Cloud Function instance that removes the external members from the group.

questions.explanation:
Google Groups settings control whether a group can contain external members. Configure each applicable group as internal by disabling the setting that allows members outside the organization; this prevents application-team group managers from adding external users. IAM allow policies and deny policies govern access to Google Cloud resources, not Google Group membership, and log-driven removal would detect violations only after they occur.

**Learn more:** [Options for limiting group access & activity](https://support.google.com/a/answer/167093?hl=en-eu) · [Changes to internal & external classifications in Google Groups](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/groups/changes-to-internal-and-external-classifications-in-google-groups)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to enforce a security policy in your Google Cloud organization that prevents users from exposing objects in their buckets externally. There are currently no buckets in the organization. Which solution should you proactively implement to meet this goal with the least operational overhead?

options.text: Create an hourly cron job to run a Cloud Function that finds public buckets and makes them private.
Enable the constraints/storage.publicAccessPrevention constraint at the organization level.
Enable the constraints/storage.uniformBucketLevelAccess constraint at the organization level.
Create a VPC Service Controls perimeter that protects the storage.googleapis.com service in your projects that contains buckets. Add any new project that contains a bucket to the perimeter.

questions.explanation:
Enforcing `constraints/storage.publicAccessPrevention` at the organization level restricts public access for all new and existing Cloud Storage buckets and objects beneath that resource. It blocks grants to public principals through IAM policies or ACLs, providing centralized, preventive enforcement without per-bucket management or remediation automation.

**Learn more:** [Public access prevention | Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/public-access-prevention) · [Organization policy constraints for Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/org-policy-constraints)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An office manager at a small startup company is responsible for reconciling payments with invoices and creating billing alerts. For compliance reasons, the office manager may have only the Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions required for these tasks. Which two IAM roles should the office manager be assigned? (Choose two.)

options.text: Organization Administrator
Project Creator

Billing Account User

The Billing Account Viewer role provides access to billing-account payment information, costs, transactions, and billing documents needed to reconcile payments and invoices. options.text: Central management of routes, firewalls, and VPNs for peered networks
Non-transitive peered networks; where only directly peered networks can communicate
Ability to peer networks that belong to different Google Cloud organizations
Firewall rules that can be created with a tag from one peered network to another peered network
Ability to share specific subnets across peered networks

questions.explanation:
VPC Network Peering is non-transitive: a VPC network can communicate with a directly peered network, but peering does not provide connectivity between two networks merely because each peers with a third network. Peering can also connect VPC networks in projects owned by different Google Cloud organizations. Peered networks exchange routes while remaining administratively separate; VPC firewall rules and network tags are not shared across the peering connection.

**Learn more:** [Google Cloud: VPC Network Peering](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/vpc-peering)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization is developing a generative AI-powered application that uses sensitive internal data to train the AI model. The application uses Vertex AI, which is generally available in your region. You must ensure that Google does not use your sensitive data when tuning public models, because doing so could cause the data to be shared with other Google Cloud customers. What should you do?

options.text: Do not use Vertex AI for sensitive data. Use only public data with minimal privacy requirements.
Encrypt your data by using customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) to have full control over encryption key access.
Do nothing. Vertex AI foundation models are frozen by default and do not use your data for model-tuning purposes.
Contact Google support to opt out of model tuning.

questions.explanation:
Google’s Vertex AI terms and documentation state that Google will not use customer data to train or fine-tune AI/ML models without the customer’s prior permission or instruction. Thus, customer data used with generally available Vertex AI foundation models is not used to tune public models by default.

**Learn more:** [Vertex AI and zero data retention](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/vertex-ai-zero-data-retention) · [Google Cloud Service Specific Terms](https://cloud.google.com/terms/service-terms)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization makes extensive use of serverless applications and prioritizes security best practices. You are responsible for enforcing image provenance and compliance with security standards before deployment. You use Cloud Build as the continuous integration and continuous deployment (CI/CD) tool to build container images. You must configure Binary Authorization so that only images built by your Cloud Build pipeline are deployed and the images pass security-standard compliance checks. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Binary Authorization attestor that uses a scanner to assess source code management repositories. Deploy images only if the attestor validates results against a security policy.
Create a Binary Authorization attestor that utilizes a scanner to evaluate container image build processes. Define a policy that requires deployment of images only if this attestation is present.
Create a Binary Authorization attestor that retrieves the Cloud Build build ID of the container image. Configure a policy to allow deployment only if there's a matching build ID attestation.
Utilize a custom Security Health Analytics module to create a policy. Enforce the policy through Binary Authorization to prevent deployment of images that do not meet predefined security standards.

questions.explanation:
Binary Authorization uses an attestor to verify a signed attestation for a specific container image at deployment time. A Cloud Build pipeline can assess the image build process for the required security and compliance conditions and produce the attestation only after those conditions pass. Requiring that attestation in the Binary Authorization policy prevents deployment of images lacking the approved build-process and compliance evidence.

**Learn more:** [Create a Binary Authorization attestation in a Cloud Build pipeline](https://cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/cloud-build) · [Attestations overview](https://cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/attestations)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],To meet data-residency requirements, you want your secrets in Google Cloud's Secret Manager to have payloads only in `europe-west1` and `europe-west4`. Your secrets must be highly available in both regions.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create your secret with a user managed replication policy, and choose only compliant locations.
Create your secret with an automatic replication policy, and choose only compliant locations.
Create two secrets by using Terraform, one in europe-west1 and the other in europe-west4.
Create your secret with an automatic replication policy, and create an organizational policy to deny secret creation in non-compliant locations.

questions.explanation:
A user-managed replication policy lets you specify the exact locations to which a secret payload is replicated. Selecting `europe-west1` and `europe-west4` restricts payload storage to those two regions while maintaining replicas in both. Automatic replication is unrestricted and therefore cannot satisfy the location constraint.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Company-approved compute images are stored in one Google Cloud project used as an image repository. This enables other projects to deploy images from the image repository project. A team needs to deploy a third-party disk image stored in an external Google Cloud organization. You need to grant read access to that disk image so it can be deployed within the perimeter.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Allow the external project by using the organizational policy, constraints/compute.trustedImageProjects.

1. Update the perimeter.2. Configure the egressTo field to include the external Google Cloud project number as an allowed resource and the serviceName to compute.googleapis.com.3. Configure the egressFrom field to set identityType to ANY_IDENTITY.

1. Update the perimeter.2. Configure the ingressFrom field to set identityType to ANY_IDENTITY.3. Configure the ingressTo field to include the external Google Cloud project number as an allowed resource and the serviceName to compute.googleapis.com.

1. Update the perimeter.2. Configure the egressTo field to set identityType to ANY_IDENTITY.3. Configure the egressFrom field to include the external Google Cloud project number as an allowed resource and the serviceName to compute.googleapis.com.

questions.explanation:

questions.question:
Your company is worried that unauthorized parties could access the Google Cloud environment through a fraudulent login page. You must deploy a solution that protects against person-in-the-middle attacks.  
  
Which security measure should you use?

options.text: Security key
Google prompt
Text message or phone call code
Google Authenticator application

questions.explanation:
A security key provides phishing-resistant authentication by using cryptographic verification tied to the legitimate login-page URL. This prevents a fraudulent site from using credentials or a second-factor response to complete authentication; SMS or voice codes, authenticator codes, and push prompts can be relayed or captured by a person-in-the-middle attacker.\
\
**Learn more:** [Titan Security Key | Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/security/products/titan-security-key?hl=en)

questions.question:
Your company is worried that unauthorized parties could access the Google Cloud environment through a fraudulent login page. You must deploy a solution that protects against person-in-the-middle attacks.  
  
Which security measure should you use?

options.text: Use Google default encryption.
Manually add users to Google Cloud.
Provision users with basic roles using Google's Identity and Access Management (IAM) service.
Use SSO/SAML integration with Cloud Identity for user authentication and user lifecycle management.
Provide granular access with predefined roles.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Identity supports SAML-based single sign-on, allowing an external identity provider to remain the authoritative authentication system and to support automated user provisioning. Google Cloud IAM predefined roles provide granular access to specific resources and are preferred over broad basic roles to follow least privilege.

**Learn more:** [Single sign-on | Cloud Architecture Center](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/identity/single-sign-on?hl=en) · [Choose which type of role to use | IAM](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/choose-role-type)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs workloads in a dedicated server room. Those workloads must be accessible only from within the private company network. You need to connect to them from Compute Engine instances in a Google Cloud Platform project.  
  
Which two approaches can meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Configure the project with Cloud VPN.
Configure the project with Shared VPC.
Configure the project with Cloud Interconnect.
Configure the project with VPC peering.
Configure all Compute Engine instances with Private Access.

questions.explanation:
Cloud VPN extends an on-premises peer network to a Google Cloud VPC using site-to-site IPsec tunnels. Cloud Interconnect connects on-premises and VPC networks through dedicated or service-provider connectivity, allowing access to VPC internal IP addresses without a VPN tunnel. Either service provides the required hybrid private-network path for Compute Engine instances to reach workloads in the server room.

**Learn more:** [Cloud VPN overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/overview) · [Cloud Interconnect overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/concepts/overview?hl=en)

Cloud NAT
Google Cloud Armor
Shielded VMs

\

Google Cloud Armor Policy rules can only match on Layer 7 (L7) attributes.
The load balancer must use the Premium Network Service Tier.
The backend service's load balancing scheme must be EXTERNAL.
The load balancer must be an external HTTP(S) load balancer.

questions.explanation:
For web-application WAF protection, a Cloud Armor security policy is attached to the backend service behind an external HTTP(S) load balancer, so it can inspect HTTP(S) requests before they reach the backend. Cloud Armor rules are not limited solely to Layer 7 attributes, and Cloud Armor can operate with either Premium or Standard Network Service Tier. Current documentation has expanded the supported load-balancing schemes beyond `EXTERNAL`, but `EXTERNAL` remains the applicable scheme for the external HTTP(S) load-balancer configuration described here.

**Learn more:** [Google Cloud Armor security policy overview](https://cloud.google.com/armor/docs/security-policy-overview)
