Your organization operates an image-classification model in production on a managed AI service in Google Cloud. During a configuration review with stakeholders, you must outline the security responsibilities for the image-classification model. What should you do?

options.text: Explain that using platform-as-a-service (PaaS) transfers security concerns to Google. Describe the need for strict API usage limits to protect against unexpected usage and billing spikes.
Explain the security aspects of the code that transforms user-uploaded images using Google's service. Define Cloud IAM for fine-grained access control within the development team.

Explain Google's shared responsibility model. Focus the configuration review on Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions, secure data upload/download procedures, and monitoring logs for any potential malicious activity.

Explain the development of custom network firewalls around the image classification service for deep intrusion detection and prevention. Describe vulnerability scanning tools for known vulnerabilities.

questions.explanation:
Security for a managed Google Cloud service follows a shared-responsibility model: Google secures the underlying service and infrastructure, while the customer remains responsible for application-level controls, IAM management, data security, and client protection. Reviewing least-privilege IAM permissions, secure image upload and download handling, and audit logs is therefore appropriate; Cloud Audit Logs records administrative activity and access to Google Cloud resources for security monitoring.

**Learn more:** [Shared responsibilities and shared fate on Google Cloud](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/security/shared-responsibility-shared-fate) · [Cloud Audit Logs overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/audit?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization enforces a custom organization policy that prevents Compute Engine VM instances from using external IP addresses. However, a regulated business unit needs an exception to temporarily use external IPs for a third-party audit process. The regulated business workload must follow least-privilege principles and minimize policy drift. You need to ensure secure policy management and appropriate handling. What should you do?

options.text: Create a folder. Apply the restrictive organization policy for non-regulated business workloads in the folder. Place the regulated business workload in that folder.

Apply the restrictive organization policy at the organization level. Create an IAM custom role with permissions to bypass organization policies. Assign the custom role to the regulated business team for the specific project.
Apply the custom organization policy at the organization level to restrict external IPs. Move the regulated business workload to a separate folder. Override the policy at that folder level.

Modify the custom organization policy at the organization level to allow external IPs for all projects. Configure VPC firewall rules to restrict egress traffic except for the regulated business workload.

questions.explanation:
Organization policies set at the organization level are inherited by descendant folders and projects, but a descendant resource can override the parent policy. Keeping the restrictive custom policy at the organization level and placing only the regulated workload in a separate folder with an override confines the temporary exception to that workload. IAM roles cannot bypass Organization Policy constraints, and relaxing the organization-level policy would unnecessarily expose other projects.

**Learn more:** [Organization Policy overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/organization-policy/overview) · [Create organization policies](https://docs.cloud.google.com/organization-policy/create-organization-policies)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing an internal App Engine application that must access a user's Google Drive on that user's behalf. Your company does not want to depend on the current user's credentials and wants to follow Google-recommended practices.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a new Service account, and give all application users the role of Service Account User.
Create a new Service account, and add all application users to a Google Group. Give this group the role of Service Account User.
Use a dedicated G Suite Admin account, and authenticate the application's operations with these G Suite credentials.
Create a new service account, and grant it G Suite domain-wide delegation. Have the application use it to impersonate the user.

questions.explanation:
Google Workspace domain-wide delegation lets a service account make API calls on behalf of users in the Workspace domain by impersonating the relevant user, without relying on that user's current credentials or individual consent. The delegation must be authorized by a domain super administrator and restricted to the required OAuth scopes, such as the Google Drive scope.

**Learn more:** [Create access credentials](https://developers.google.com/workspace/guides/create-credentials) · [Using OAuth 2.0 for Server to Server Applications](https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/service-account)

questions.question: Your company's cloud-security policy requires that VM instances not have external IP addresses. You need to determine which Google Cloud service enables VM instances without external IP addresses to connect to the internet to update the VMs. Which service should you use?

options.text: Identity Aware-Proxy
Cloud NAT
TCP/UDP Load Balancing
Cloud DNS

questions.explanation:
Cloud NAT supplies source NAT for outbound connections from VM instances that have only internal IP addresses, allowing them to reach internet update services without assigning external IP addresses to the VMs. It permits return traffic for those established outbound connections but does not allow unsolicited inbound internet connections.\
\
**Learn more:** [Cloud NAT overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/nat/docs/overview)

questions.question: Your company's cloud-security policy requires that VM instances not have external IP addresses. You need to determine which Google Cloud service enables VM instances without external IP addresses to connect to the internet to update the VMs. Which service should you use?

options.text: Secret Manager
Cloud Key Management Service
Cloud Data Loss Prevention with cryptographic hashing
Cloud Data Loss Prevention with automatic text redaction
Cloud Data Loss Prevention with deterministic encryption using AES-SIV

questions.explanation:
Cloud Data Loss Prevention deterministic encryption using AES-SIV provides reversible de-identification, allowing the same PII values to be obfuscated and later re-identified with the original cryptographic key. Cloud Key Management Service supplies the key-management and key-wrapping capability used by this workflow. Cryptographic hashing and automatic text redaction cannot be reversed.

**Learn more:** [De-identify and re-identify sensitive data](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/inspect-sensitive-text-de-identify) · [Pseudonymization](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/pseudonymization)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are creating a new governance model for your organization's secrets stored in Secret Manager. At present, Production and Non-Production application secrets are stored and accessed by using service accounts. The proposed solution must:  
  
- Provide granular access to secrets  
- Give you control over the rotation schedules for the encryption keys that wrap your secrets  
- Preserve environment separation  
- Provide ease of management  
  
Which approach should you take?

options.text: 1. Use separate Google Cloud projects to store Production and Non-Production secrets. 2. Enforce access control to secrets using project-level identity and Access Management (IAM) bindings. 3. Use customer-managed encryption keys to encrypt secrets.

1. Use a single Google Cloud project to store both Production and Non-Production secrets. 2. Enforce access control to secrets using secret-level Identity and Access Management (IAM) bindings. 3. Use Google-managed encryption keys to encrypt secrets.

1. Use separate Google Cloud projects to store Production and Non-Production secrets. 2. Enforce access control to secrets using secret-level Identity and Access Management (IAM) bindings. 3. Use Google-managed encryption keys to encrypt secrets.

1. Use a single Google Cloud project to store both Production and Non-Production secrets. 2. Enforce access control to secrets using project-level Identity and Access Management (IAM) bindings. 3. Use customer-managed encryption keys to encrypt secrets.

questions.explanation:
Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) in Cloud KMS give customers control over key rotation schedules, lifecycle, usage, and permissions, whereas Google-managed encryption does not. Storing Production and Non-Production secrets in separate projects preserves environment isolation, while project-level IAM policies offer a simpler administration model for each environment. [Enable customer-managed encryption keys for Secret Manager](https://docs.cloud.google.com/secret-manager/docs/cmek)

**Learn more:** [Enable customer-managed encryption keys for Secret Manager](https://docs.cloud.google.com/secret-manager/docs/cmek) · [Access control with IAM](https://docs.cloud.google.com/secret-manager/docs/access-control)

Your company’s storage team manages every product image in a particular Google Cloud project. To retain control, you need to isolate Cloud Storage access for this project so the storage team can manage restrictions at the project level. They must be limited to corporate computers. What should you do?

options.text: Use Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles at the project level within the storage team’s project. Grant the storage team granular permissions on the project’s Cloud Storage resources.
Employ organization-level firewall rules to block all traffic to Cloud Storage. Create exceptions for specific service accounts used by the storage team within their project.

Use Context-Aware Access Create an access level that defines the required context. Apply it as an organization policy specifically at the project level, restricting access to Cloud Storage based on that context.

Implement VPC Service Controls by establishing an organization-wide service perimeter with all projects. Configure ingress and egress rules to restrict access to Cloud Storage based on IP address ranges.

questions.explanation:
Context-Aware Access can enforce access requirements using attributes such as device state, network, location, and user identity. Creating an access level that represents compliant corporate computers and applying that context-based restriction to the relevant project provides device-aware control for Cloud Storage access without imposing an organization-wide perimeter on all projects. [Set up Context-Aware Access](https://cloud.google.com/access-context-manager/docs/securing-console-and-apis)

You must make sure that the keys used for at-rest encryption of your data comply with your organization's security controls. One security control requires keys to be rotated every 90 days. You need to implement an effective detection strategy to verify that keys are rotated as required. What should you do?

options.text: Analyze the crypto key versions of the keys by using data from Cloud Asset Inventory. If an active key is older than 90 days, send an alert message through your incident notification channel.
Assess the keys in the Cloud Key Management Service by implementing code in Cloud Run. If a key is not rotated after 90 days, raise a finding in Security Command Center.
Define a metric that checks for timely key updates by using Cloud Logging. If a key is not rotated after 90 days, send an alert message through your incident notification channel.
Identify keys that have not been rotated by using Security Health Analytics. If a key is not rotated after 90 days, a finding in Security Command Center is raised.

questions.explanation:
Security Health Analytics has a built-in `KMS_KEY_NOT_ROTATED` detector that checks Cloud KMS keys against a 90-day rotation requirement and generates a Security Command Center finding when the requirement is not met. This provides managed, continuous compliance detection for the specified rotation control.

**Learn more:** [Code a custom module for Security Health Analytics](https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/custom-modules-sha-code) · [Use Security Health Analytics](https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-use-security-health-analytics)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization is using a third-party identity and authentication provider to centrally manage users. You want to use this identity provider to grant access to the Google Cloud console without synchronizing identities to Google Cloud. Users must receive permissions based on attributes. What should you do?

options.text: Configure the central identity provider as a workforce identity pool provider in Workforce Identity Federation. Create an attribute mapping by using the Common Expression Language (CEL).
Configure a periodic synchronization of relevant users and groups with attributes to Cloud Identity. Activate single sign-on by using the Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML).
Set up the Google Cloud Identity Platform. Configure an external authentication provider by using OpenID Connect and link user accounts based on attributes.
Activate external identities on the Identity-Aware Proxy. Use the Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) to configure authentication based on attributes to the central authentication provider.

questions.explanation:
Workforce Identity Federation provides syncless, attribute-based single sign-on for workforce users through an external identity provider. A workforce identity pool provider can map identity-provider claims to Google and custom attributes using Common Expression Language (CEL), enabling IAM authorization based on those attributes.

**Learn more:** [Workforce Identity Federation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/workforce-identity-federation) · [Configure Workforce Identity Federation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/configuring-workforce-identity-federation)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],As part of your organization’s zero-trust strategy, you use Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) to secure multiple applications. You need to ingest logs into a Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) system so that you receive alerts about possible intrusions.  
  
Which logs should you analyze?

options.text: Data Access audit logs
Policy Denied audit logs
Cloud Identity user log events
Admin Activity audit logs

questions.explanation:
IAP records authorized and unauthorized requests to protected resources in Data Access audit logs. These logs contain useful intrusion-detection details, including the authenticated principal when present, caller IP address, requested resource and URL, and whether IAP granted the requested access.

**Learn more:** [Identity-Aware Proxy audit logging](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iap/docs/audit-log-howto) · [Setting up context-aware access with Identity-Aware Proxy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iap/docs/cloud-iap-context-aware-access-howto)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You run applications outside Google Cloud that require access to Google Cloud resources. You use workload identity federation to assign external identities Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, removing the maintenance and security burden of service account keys. You must guard against attempts to spoof another user's identity and obtain unauthorized access to Google Cloud resources.  
  
What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Enable data access logs for IAM APIs.
Limit the number of external identities that can impersonate a service account.
Use a dedicated project to manage workload identity pools and providers.
Use immutable attributes in attribute mappings.
Limit the resources that a service account can access.

questions.explanation:
A dedicated project centralizes control of workload identity pools and providers, helping ensure trusted providers and consistent mappings. Attribute mappings must use immutable attributes because user-modifiable attributes can be changed to match an existing IAM binding and thereby enable identity spoofing.

**Learn more:** [Best practices for using Workload Identity Federation](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/best-practices-for-using-workload-identity-federation)

questions.domain: Securing communications and establishing boundary protection
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An engineering team is deploying a web application that will be publicly accessible on the internet. The web application is hosted across multiple GCP regions and will be routed to the appropriate backend based on the URL request.  
  
The team wants to prevent direct internet exposure of the application and deny traffic from a specified list of malicious IP addresses.  
  
Which solution should the team implement to meet these requirements?

options.text: Cloud Armor
Network Load Balancing
SSL Proxy Load Balancing
NAT Gateway

questions.explanation:
Cloud Armor applies security policies at the Google Cloud edge to applications behind supported load balancers. Its rules can deny requests from specified source IP addresses, while the load balancer fronts the multi-region backends so the application instances do not need direct public exposure. [Cloud Armor security policy use cases](https://cloud.google.com/armor/docs/common-use-cases)

**Learn more:** [Cloud Armor security policy use cases](https://cloud.google.com/armor/docs/common-use-cases) · [Cloud Armor overview](https://cloud.google.com/armor/docs/cloud-armor-overview)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An application running on a Compute Engine instance must read data from a Cloud Storage bucket. Your team does not permit Cloud Storage buckets to be globally readable and wants to enforce the principle of least privilege.  
  
Which option satisfies your team’s requirement?

options.text: Create a Cloud Storage ACL that allows read-only access from the Compute Engine instance's IP address and allows the application to read from the bucket without credentials.
Use a service account with read-only access to the Cloud Storage bucket, and store the credentials to the service account in the config of the application on the Compute Engine instance.
Use a service account with read-only access to the Cloud Storage bucket to retrieve the credentials from the instance metadata.
Encrypt the data in the Cloud Storage bucket using Cloud KMS, and allow the application to decrypt the data with the KMS key.

questions.explanation:
An attached service account can be granted only the Cloud Storage read permissions required for the bucket, while the application obtains short-lived access credentials through the Compute Engine metadata server. This avoids making the bucket public and avoids storing long-lived service-account credentials in application configuration.

**Learn more:** [Service accounts | Compute Engine](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/access/service-accounts) · [Authenticate workloads to Google Cloud APIs using service accounts](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/access/authenticate-workloads)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An organization adopts Google Cloud Platform (GCP) for application-hosting services and requires guidance for configuring password requirements for its Cloud Identity account. The organization’s password policy requires corporate employee passwords to have a minimum number of characters.  
  
Which Cloud Identity password guideline can the organization use to inform its new requirements?

options.text: Set the minimum length for passwords to be 8 characters.
Set the minimum length for passwords to be 10 characters.
Set the minimum length for passwords to be 12 characters.
Set the minimum length for passwords to be 6 characters.

questions.explanation:
Google’s password guidance recommends using passwords of at least 12 characters because longer passwords are stronger. Cloud Identity password policies can enforce configurable minimum and maximum lengths, including a 12-character minimum.

**Learn more:** [Create a strong password & a more secure account](https://support.google.com/a/answer/32040?hl=en) · [Apply and monitor password requirements for users](https://support.google.com/cloudidentity/answer/139399?hl=en)

questions.domain: Securing communications and establishing boundary protection
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An organization is migrating from its existing on-premises productivity software systems to G Suite. Certain network security controls were required by a regional regulatory body for the previous on-premises system. The organization's risk team wants to make sure that network security controls remain in place and effective in G Suite.  
  
A security architect supporting the migration has been asked to ensure that network security controls are addressed under the new shared-responsibility model between the organization and Google Cloud.  
  
What solution would help satisfy these requirements?

options.text: Ensure that firewall rules are in place to meet the required controls.
Set up Cloud Armor to ensure that network security controls can be managed for G Suite.
Network security is a built-in solution and Google's Cloud responsibility for SaaS products like G Suite.
Set up an array of Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networks to control network security as mandated by the relevant regulation.

questions.explanation:
G Suite is a SaaS product, so Google is responsible for securing the underlying network and infrastructure. Customer-managed firewall rules, Cloud Armor, and VPC networks apply to customer-managed Google Cloud workloads rather than the Google-managed G Suite service. The customer remains responsible for access controls and the data it stores in the service.

**Learn more:** [Shared responsibilities and shared fate on Google Cloud](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/security/shared-responsibility-shared-fate)

questions.domain: Securing communications and establishing boundary protection
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You recently joined the networking team that supports your company’s Google Cloud implementation. You are responsible for becoming familiar with the firewall-rule configuration and making recommendations based on your networking and Google Cloud experience. Which product should you recommend to detect firewall rules whose attributes are overlapped by other firewall rules with higher or equal priority?

options.text: Security Command Center
Firewall Rules Logging
VPC Flow Logs
Firewall Insights

questions.explanation:
Firewall Insights detects shadowed firewall rules. A shadowed rule has relevant attributes, such as IP address ranges or ports, that are overlapped by one or more firewall rules with higher or equal priority.

**Learn more:** [Firewall Insights overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-intelligence-center/docs/firewall-insights/concepts/overview) · [Troubleshoot policy and access problems](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/troubleshooting-policy-and-access-problems)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage a Google Cloud environment organized into folders representing different teams. The teams require flexibility to change organization policies that pertain to their work. You want to give them the needed permissions while maintaining Google-recommended security practices and minimizing administrative complexity. What should you do?

options.text: Create a custom IAM role with the organization policy administrator permission and grant the permission to each team’s folder. Limit policy modifications based on folder names within the custom role’s definition.
Assign the organization policy administrator role to a central service account and provide teams with the credentials to use the service account when needed.
Create an organization-level tag. Attach the tag to relevant folders. Use an IAM condition to restrict the organization policy administrator role to resources with that tag.
Grant each team the organization policy administrator role at the organization level.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud supports delegating Organization Policy Administrator (`roles/orgpolicy.policyAdmin`) through an IAM Condition on its role binding. Tagging the relevant folders and making the binding conditional on that tag limits each team’s policy-management authority to the appropriate resources, while retaining the predefined role and centralized access-control management.

**Learn more:** [Scope organization policies with tags](https://cloud.google.com/organization-policy/docs/scope-policies) · [Tags and conditional access](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/tags-access-control)

questions.domain: Securing communications and establishing boundary protection
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization runs Google Cloud applications that need to access external web services. You must monitor, control, and log access to those services. What should you do?

options.text: Set up a Secure Web Proxy that allows access to the specific external web services. Configure applications to use the proxy for the web service requests.
Set up a Cloud NAT instance to allow egress traffic from your VPC.
Configure VPC firewall rules to allow the services to access the IP addresses of required external web services.
Configure Google Cloud Armor to monitor and protect your applications by checking incoming traffic patterns for attack patterns.

questions.explanation:
Secure Web Proxy centrally mediates outbound HTTP and HTTPS requests from cloud workloads. Its policies can restrict access to approved external web services, and its proxy transaction logs are written to Cloud Logging, providing the required monitoring, control, and auditability.

**Learn more:** [Secure Web Proxy overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/secure-web-proxy/docs/overview) · [Logs and metrics | Secure Web Proxy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/secure-web-proxy/docs/monitor-logs)

questions.question: When building a secure container image, which two items should you include where possible? (Choose two.)

options.text: Ensure that the app does not run as PID 1.
Package a single app as a container.
Remove any unnecessary tools not needed by the app.
Use public container images as a base image for the app.
Use many container image layers to hide sensitive information.

questions.explanation:
A secure container image should contain one focused application or service per container and exclude tools that the application does not need. This reduces complexity, dependencies, and attack surface.\
\
**Learn more:** [Docker Docs: Building best practices](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/best-practices/)

options.text: Create a single KeyRing for all persistent disks and all Keys in this KeyRing. Manage the IAM permissions at the Key level.
Create a single KeyRing for all persistent disks and all Keys in this KeyRing. Manage the IAM permissions at the KeyRing level.
Create a KeyRing per persistent disk, with each KeyRing containing a single Key. Manage the IAM permissions at the Key level.
Create a KeyRing per persistent disk, with each KeyRing containing a single Key. Manage the IAM permissions at the KeyRing level.

questions.explanation:
Cloud KMS keys are contained in KeyRings, and IAM roles granted on a KeyRing apply to all keys in that KeyRing. Placing the persistent-disk keys in one KeyRing and managing IAM there provides one shared permission policy for every key.

**Learn more:** [Cloud KMS access control with IAM](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kms/docs/iam?hl=en) · [Cloud KMS permissions and roles](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kms/docs/reference/permissions-and-roles)

Your company has been manually creating users in Cloud Identity to grant access to Google Cloud resources. Because the environment continues to grow, you want to authorize the Google Cloud Directory Sync (GCDS) instance and integrate it with the on-premises LDAP server to onboard hundreds of users. You are required to:  
  
- Replicate user and group lifecycle changes from the on-premises LDAP server to Cloud Identity.  
- Disable any users that were manually created in Cloud Identity.  
  
You have already configured the LDAP search attributes to include the users and security groups that are in scope for Google Cloud. What should you do next to complete this solution?

options.text: 1. Configure the option to suspend domain users not found in LDAP. 2. Set up a recurring GCDS task.
1. Configure the option to delete domain users not found in LDAP. 2. Run GCDS after user and group lifecycle changes.
1. Configure the LDAP search attributes to exclude manually created Cloud Identity users not found in LDAP. 2. Set up a recurring GCDS task.
1. Configure the LDAP search attributes to exclude manually created Cloud Identity users not found in LDAP. 2. Run GCDS after user and group lifecycle changes.

questions.explanation:
GCDS must be configured to suspend domain users that are not found in LDAP, because manually created Cloud Identity users are absent from the authoritative LDAP source and suspension satisfies the requirement to disable them without deleting them. A recurring GCDS task continuously applies user and group lifecycle changes from LDAP. Google’s documentation describes suspending users that are absent from the external directory and distinguishes this from deletion.

**Learn more:** [Set up user sync — Cloud Identity Help](https://support.google.com/cloudidentity/answer/10344342?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization uses Cloud Run services across multiple projects beneath the non-production folder and requires primarily internal communication. Some services require external access to approved fully qualified domain names (FQDNs), while all other external traffic must be blocked. Internal applications must not be exposed. You must provide this granular control, with allowlists overriding broader restrictions only for designated VPCs. What should you do?

options.text: Implement a global-level allowlist rule for the necessary FQDNs within a hierarchical firewall policy. Apply this policy across all VPCs in the organization and configure Cloud NAT without any additional filtering.

Create a folder-level deny-all rule for outbound traffic within a hierarchical firewall policy. Define FQDN allowlist rules in separate policies and associate them with the necessary VPCs. Configure Cloud NAT for these VPCs.

Create a project-level deny-all rule within a hierarchical structure and apply it broadly. Override this rule with separate FQDN allowlists defined in VPC-level firewall policies associated with the relevant VPCs.
Configure Cloud NAT with IP-based filtering to permit outbound traffic only to the allowlist d FQDNs' IP ranges. Apply Cloud NAT uniformly to all VPCs within the organization's folder structure.

questions.explanation:
Cloud NGFW supports FQDN objects in firewall-policy rules for domain-based traffic control. A restrictive egress baseline can be applied at the non-production folder, with higher-priority FQDN allow rules scoped to the VPC networks that need those destinations; all remaining external traffic is denied. Cloud NAT supplies outbound internet connectivity for the permitted VPCs but does not itself filter traffic by FQDN. Hierarchical policies are applied at the organization or folder level, whereas VPC-associated network firewall policies cannot override a higher-level deny rule.

**Learn more:** [Hierarchical firewall policies](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewall-policies) · [Fully qualified domain name objects overview](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/fqdn-objects-overview)

questions.question:
Your company uses GSuite and has developed an application for internal use on Google App Engine. You must ensure that an external user cannot access the application even if an employee's password is compromised.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Enforce 2-factor authentication in GSuite for all users.
Configure Cloud Identity-Aware Proxy for the App Engine Application.
Provision user passwords using GSuite Password Sync.
Configure Cloud VPN between your private network and GCP.

questions.explanation:
Two-factor authentication requires a second verification factor in addition to the employee’s password. Therefore, a stolen password alone cannot be used to sign in and access the internal application.\
\
**Learn more:** [Protect your business with 2-Step Verification](https://support.google.com/a/answer/175197?hl=en-GI)

questions.question:
Your company uses GSuite and has developed an application for internal use on Google App Engine. You must ensure that an external user cannot access the application even if an employee's password is compromised.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use the Cloud Key Management Service to manage the data encryption key (DEK).
Use the Cloud Key Management Service to manage the key encryption key (KEK).
Use customer-supplied encryption keys to manage the data encryption key (DEK).
Use customer-supplied encryption keys to manage the key encryption key (KEK).

questions.explanation:
Cloud Dataproc customer-managed encryption keys use Cloud Key Management Service to manage the key encryption key (KEK). The service retains management of the data encryption keys (DEKs) that encrypt the persistent-disk data, while Cloud KMS lets the customer manage the KEK lifecycle, including rotation and destruction.

**Learn more:** [Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) | Dataproc](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dataproc/docs/concepts/configuring-clusters/customer-managed-encryption) · [Envelope encryption | Cloud Key Management Service](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kms/docs/envelope-encryption)

You want to validate these policy changes before they are enforced. Which service should you use?

An organization is building an application that will serve both corporate and public end users. The organization wants to centrally manage these customers’ identities and authorizations. Corporate end users must be able to access the application by using their corporate username and domain. What should you do?

options.text: Add the corporate and public end-user domains to domain restricted sharing on the organization.
Federate the customers' identity provider (IdP) with Workforce Identity Federation in your application's project.
Do nothing. Google Workspace identities will allow you to filter personal accounts and disable their access.
Use a customer identity and access management tool (CIAM) like Identity Platform.

questions.explanation:
Identity Platform is a customer identity and access management (CIAM) service for application users. It centrally manages customer authentication and access and can integrate corporate users through external identity providers while also supporting public users. Workforce Identity Federation instead enables a workforce to access Google Cloud resources through an external identity provider.

**Learn more:** [Identity Platform](https://cloud.google.com/security/products/identity-platform) · [Identities for users](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/user-identities)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You run code in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) containers on Google Cloud that needs access to objects stored in a Cloud Storage bucket. You need to securely give the Pods access to the bucket while minimizing management overhead. What should you do?

options.text: Create a service account. Grant bucket access to the Pods by using Workload Identity Federation for GKE.
Create a service account with keys. Store the keys in Secret Manager with a 30-day rotation schedule. Reference the keys in the Pods.
Create a service account with keys. Store the keys as a Kubernetes secret. Reference the keys in the Pods.
Create a service account with keys. Store the keys in Secret Manager. Reference the keys in the Pods.

questions.explanation:
Workload Identity Federation for GKE lets Pods authenticate to Google Cloud services through IAM using short-lived credentials, so Cloud Storage bucket permissions can be granted without creating, distributing, storing, or rotating service-account keys. Google Cloud recommends it for GKE workloads accessing Cloud Storage and other Google Cloud resources.

**Learn more:** [Authenticate to GKE](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/authentication) · [About Workload Identity Federation for GKE](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/workload-identity)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A vendor requires access to your company’s Google Cloud environment. The vendor uses a third-party identity provider (IdP). You must integrate this IdP with your company’s Google Cloud environment to provide single sign-on (SSO) for the vendor’s users in the most secure manner. You do not want to manage any vendor user lifecycle management. What should you do?

options.text: Use Google Cloud Directory Sync to synchronize user accounts from the IdP to Google Workspace, and then configure SSO between Google Workspace and Google Cloud.
Develop a custom application that queries the IdP for user authentication and then programmatically creates Google Cloud user accounts.
Connect the vendor's IdP with Google Cloud using Workforce Identify Federation.
Create Google Cloud accounts for each user and synchronize their passwords with the third-party IdP.

questions.explanation:
Workforce Identity Federation lets external workforce users, including partners and contractors, authenticate through their own third-party IdP and access Google Cloud by SSO. It is syncless, so Google Cloud does not store or require synchronized Google-managed user accounts; the vendor retains responsibility for user lifecycle management.

**Learn more:** [Workforce Identity Federation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/workforce-identity-federation) · [Identities for users](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/user-identities)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company has deployed an application on Compute Engine. Clients can access the application on port 587. You need to distribute load across the different instances running the application. The connection must be secured with TLS and terminated at the Load Balancer.  
  
Which type of Load Balancing should you use?

options.text: Network Load Balancing
HTTP(S) Load Balancing
TCP Proxy Load Balancing
SSL Proxy Load Balancing

questions.explanation:
SSL Proxy Load Balancing is designed for non-HTTP TCP traffic that requires TLS termination at the load-balancing layer. It terminates the client TLS connection and proxies the resulting TCP connection to a selected backend instance. Port 587 is not HTTP(S) traffic, so HTTP(S) Load Balancing does not apply; a passthrough network load balancer would not perform TLS termination.

**Learn more:** [Proxy Network Load Balancer overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/proxy-network-load-balancer) · [SSL policies overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/ssl-policies-concepts)
